docs.title: Ethical Hacking Concepts
docs.text: Ethical hackers follow the same processes as malicious actors, learning to gain and maintain access to systems in identical ways. The difference lies only in authorization and intent. This section provides an overview of ethical hacking, explains why it is necessary, covers its scope and limitations, and details the skills required of ethical hackers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Ethical hacking is the practice of employing computer and network skills to help organizations test their network security for vulnerabilities. It involves using the same hacking tools, tricks, and techniques as malicious attackers — but with explicit permission from the system or network owner and without intent to cause harm.

Practitioners are called White Hats (also: security analysts or ethical hackers). All discovered vulnerabilities are reported to the owner for remediation.

docs.title: Key Terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Hacker (noun) Person who enjoys learning the details of computer systems and stretching their capabilities To hack (verb) Rapid development of new programs or reverse engineering existing software to improve it Cracker / Attacker Person who employs hacking skills for offensive (illegal) purposes Ethical hacker Security professional who employs hacking skills for defensive purposes

docs.title: Why Ethical Hacking Is Necessary
docs.text:
"To beat a hacker, you need to think like one!"

Ethical hacking is necessary because it allows organizations to counter attacks from malicious hackers by anticipating the methods used to break into systems. Vulnerability testing and security audits alone cannot guarantee network security — hacking requires creative thinking. Organizations must adopt a defense-in-depth strategy by penetrating their own networks to expose vulnerabilities before attackers do.

docs.title: Reasons Organizations Recruit Ethical Hackers
docs.text:
• Prevent hackers from gaining access to information systems
  • Uncover vulnerabilities and assess their potential as a security risk
  • Analyze and strengthen the organization's security posture (policies, network protection, end-user practices)
  • Provide preventive measures to avoid security breaches
  • Safeguard customer data
  • Enhance security awareness at all levels in the business

docs.title: Three Questions an Ethical Hacker Must Answer
docs.text:
1. What can an attacker see on the target system? Standard admin checks often overlook what is visible during reconnaissance and scanning phases.

  2. What can an intruder do with that information? The ethical hacker must anticipate intent and purpose to determine appropriate countermeasures during the gaining-access and maintaining-access phases.

  3. Are the attackers' attempts being noticed? Attackers may persist for days, weeks, or months before acting. During reconnaissance and covering-tracks phases, the ethical hacker should detect and stop the intrusion.

docs.title: Process Scope Questions
docs.text:
The entire ethical hacking process depends on agreed answers to:

  • What is the organization trying to protect?
  • Against whom or what are they protecting it?
  • Are all components adequately protected, updated, and patched?
  • How much time, effort, and money is the client willing to invest?
  • Do security measures comply with industry and legal standards?

Key principle: It is never possible to guard systems completely — but they can always be improved. The ethical hacker and client must agree on a framework before the evaluation begins.

docs.title: Ethical Hackers vs. Crackers
docs.text:
The critical differentiator is consent:

  • Crackers attempt unauthorized access and conceal their activities.
  • Ethical hackers are fully transparent about what they are doing and how — always operating under a legal agreement.

Ethical hackers use the same tools as attackers but do not damage the system. Their output: a vulnerability assessment and remediation recommendations for administrators.

docs.title: Scope and Limitations of Ethical Hacking
Scope
docs.text:
Ethical hacking is a structured, organized security assessment — typically part of a penetration test or security audit. It is a crucial component of:

  • Risk assessment
  • Auditing and counter fraud
  • Information systems security best practices

It is used to identify risks, highlight remedial actions, and reduce ICT costs by resolving vulnerabilities.

Many ethical hackers operate as part of a Tiger Team — a group that performs full-scale testing covering all network, physical, and system intrusion aspects.

docs.title: Rules Ethical Hackers Must Follow
docs.text:
• Gain written authorization — no activities begin without a signed legal document granting express permission.
  • Maintain confidentiality — sign and adhere to a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA); never disclose sensitive information or test details to third parties.
  • Stay within agreed limits — e.g., perform DoS attacks only if explicitly agreed upon; exceeding scope can cause revenue loss, reputational damage, and legal consequences.

docs.title: Security Audit Framework (Steps)
docs.text:
1. Discuss client needs and define scope
  2. Prepare and sign NDA documents
  3. Organize the ethical hacking team and schedule
  4. Conduct the test
  5. Analyze results and prepare a report
  6. Present findings to the client

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The organization must know what they are looking for before hiring an outside vendor — otherwise little value is gained.
  • An ethical hacker can only help the organization understand its security system; placing the right safeguards is the organization's responsibility.

docs.title: AI-Driven Ethical Hacking
docs.text:
AI-driven ethical hacking is a modern approach where AI technologies (algorithms, machine learning models, and automation frameworks) are used to enhance the capabilities of ethical hackers — making the process more efficient, scalable, and effective.

As hackers increasingly leverage AI to automate and augment attacks, ethical hackers use the same technologies to anticipate emerging threats, outpace malicious actors, and proactively mitigate risks.

docs.title: Benefits of AI in Ethical Hacking
docs.text: Benefit Description Efficiency Quickly processes large amounts of data, speeding up the hacking process Accuracy Reduces human error and increases the accuracy of vulnerability assessments Scalability Handles the growing complexity and volume of cyberthreats Cost-Effectiveness Automation and efficiency gains reduce overall cybersecurity costs

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
• Network Security — Monitoring traffic for suspicious activities and potential breaches
  • Application Security — Testing web and mobile apps with AI-powered tools
  • Cloud Security — Identifying and mitigating risks in cloud environments
  • IoT Security — Protecting IoT devices from cyberthreats
  • Threat Intelligence — Gathering and analyzing threat data for actionable insights

docs.title: How AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Helps Ethical Hackers
docs.text:
AI enhances the efficiency, effectiveness, and scope of cybersecurity measures, giving ethical hackers powerful tools to defend against sophisticated threats.

# Capability Description 1 Automation of Repetitive Tasks Automates scanning, traffic monitoring, and threat identification — freeing hackers for complex tasks 2 Predictive Analysis ML models learn from past attacks to predict future threats and identify anomalies proactively 3 Advanced Threat Detection Detects zero-day vulnerabilities and subtle indicators of compromise via deep learning and anomaly detection 4 Enhanced Decision Making Provides data-driven insights and recommendations for resource allocation and threat response 5 Adaptive Learning Continuously learns from new attack types and updates detection/response strategies automatically 6 Enhanced Reporting Generates detailed, accurate vulnerability reports to help prioritize security efforts 7 Simulation and Testing Simulates real-world attacks to test system resilience and identify defensive weaknesses 8 Scalability Handles large-scale and complex environments more efficiently than manual methods 9 Continuous Monitoring Monitors and assesses security postures in real time rather than during periodic reviews 10 Adaptive Defense Mechanisms Updates algorithms and response strategies to counteract the latest hacking techniques

docs.title: Myth: AI Will Replace Ethical Hackers
docs.text:
AI-driven ethical hacking is a valuable tool in the arsenal of ethical hackers — not a replacement.

  • AI can automate certain tasks and improve efficiency, but human expertise, creativity, and critical thinking remain indispensable.
  • Ethical hacking involves a complex interplay of technical skills, domain knowledge, and ethical considerations that go beyond the capabilities of AI systems alone.
  • Ethical hackers possess deep understanding of systems and networks, the ability to think like attackers, identify entry points, and craft tailored mitigation strategies — something AI cannot replicate.
  • AI tools assist by automating routine tasks, but human oversight is essential to interpret results, validate findings, and make informed judgments based on contextual knowledge and ethical principles.
  • The optimal outcome is AI + human collaboration: combining machine efficiency with human creativity strengthens cybersecurity defenses against a diverse and evolving threat landscape.

docs.title: Flashcards – Module 01
docs.text:
Question

What is the definition of information security?

Answer

The state of well-being of information and infrastructure in which the possibility of theft, tampering, and disruption of information and services is low or tolerable.

→ Information Security Overview Question

What is an asset in information security?

Answer

Any physical device or digital resource belonging to an organization that holds or processes valuable information. Examples include hardware, software, data, network resources, and people.

→ What are Assets? Question

What are the five elements of information security?

Answer

Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, Authenticity, Non-Repudiation (CIA + AN).

→ Elements of Information Security Question

What is Confidentiality and what controls enforce it?

Answer

Assurance that information is accessible only to authorized users. Controls: data classification, encryption, secure disposal of equipment.

→ Elements of Information Security Question

What is Integrity and what controls enforce it?

Answer

Trustworthiness of data; prevention of improper or unauthorized changes. Controls: checksums, access control.

→ Elements of Information Security Question

What is Availability and what controls enforce it?

Answer

Systems are accessible when required by authorized users. Controls: redundant disk arrays, clustered machines, antivirus, DDoS prevention systems.

→ Elements of Information Security Question

What is Authenticity and what controls enforce it?

Answer

Ensures data and communications are genuine and uncorrupted. Controls: biometrics, smart cards, digital certificates.

→ Elements of Information Security Question

What is Non-Repudiation and how is it enforced?

Answer

Guarantee that the sender cannot deny sending a message and the recipient cannot deny receiving it. Enforced via digital signatures.

→ Elements of Information Security Question

What is the attack formula in information security?

Answer

Attack = Motive (Goal) + Method (TTP) + Vulnerability

→ Attacks: Motives, Goals, and Objectives Question

What is an "attack" in the context of information security?

Answer

An action performed to breach an IT system's security by exploiting vulnerabilities — obtaining, editing, removing, destroying, or revealing information without authorization.

→ Attacks: Motives, Goals, and Objectives Question

Where does an attacker's motive originate?

Answer

From the notion that the target system stores or processes something valuable, leading to the threat of an attack.

→ Motives Behind Attacks Question

Name at least five common motives behind information security attacks.

Answer

Disrupting business continuity, information theft, financial loss, damaging reputation, demanding ransom, revenge, propagating beliefs, military objectives, disrupting critical infrastructure.

→ Motives Behind Attacks Question

What does TTP stand for and what does it refer to?

Answer

Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures — the patterns of activities and methods associated with specific threat actors or groups.

→ TTPs Question

Distinguish: Tactics vs. Techniques vs. Procedures

Answer

Tactics: the overall strategy from start to finish. Techniques: technical methods to achieve intermediate results. Procedures: the systematic approach used to launch an attack.

→ TTPs Question

Why is understanding TTPs valuable for defenders?

Answer

Tactics → predict/detect threats early. Techniques → identify vulnerabilities and implement countermeasures. Procedures → reveal what the attacker targets in the infrastructure.

→ TTPs Question

What is a vulnerability in information security?

Answer

A weakness in the design or implementation of a system that can be exploited to compromise security — often allowing an attacker to bypass authentication. Root causes: misconfiguration and poor programming practices.

→ Vulnerability Question

What is the difference between a weakness and a vulnerability?

Answer

Weakness: a flaw that reduces security but is not necessarily exploitable. Vulnerability: a weakness that can be exploited by a threat actor via a known method. Every vulnerability is a weakness — not every weakness is a vulnerability.

→ Weakness vs. Vulnerability Question

Name the five common reasons for the existence of vulnerabilities.

Answer

1. Hardware/software misconfiguration 2. Insecure or poor network/application design 3. Inherent technology weaknesses 4. End-user carelessness 5. Intentional end-user acts

→ Common Reasons for Vulnerabilities Question

How does hardware or software misconfiguration create vulnerabilities?

Answer

Insecure configs create security loopholes — e.g., unencrypted protocols expose data in transit; misconfigured hardware grants unauthorized network access; misconfigured software exposes applications and data.

→ Common Reasons for Vulnerabilities Question

How does insecure network or application design create vulnerabilities?

Answer

Improperly implemented firewalls, IDS, or VPNs expose the network to numerous threats and potential data loss.

→ Common Reasons for Vulnerabilities Question

What are inherent technology weaknesses and why are they dangerous?

Answer

Hardware or software that cannot defend against certain attack types (e.g., DoS, MitM). Outdated browsers or unpatched systems are prone to distributed attacks and malware.

→ Common Reasons for Vulnerabilities Question

How does end-user carelessness create vulnerabilities?

Answer

Sharing credentials, connecting to insecure networks, and falling for social engineering attacks — all leading to data loss or information leakage.

→ Common Reasons for Vulnerabilities Question

What are intentional end-user acts and what is an example?

Answer

Deliberate misuse by insiders — e.g., ex-employees who retain access to shared drives and leak sensitive company information, causing data and financial loss.

→ Common Reasons for Vulnerabilities Question

What are examples of technological vulnerabilities?

Answer

TCP/IP protocols (HTTP, FTP, ICMP, SNMP, SMTP are inherently insecure); unpatched or inherently insecure OSes; network devices lacking authentication, password protection, or using insecure routing protocols.

→ Technological Vulnerabilities Question

What are examples of configuration vulnerabilities?

Answer

Insecure transmission of user credentials; weak system account passwords; misconfigured internet services (IIS, Apache, FTP); default passwords/settings left unchanged; misconfigured network devices.

→ Configuration Vulnerabilities Question

According to IATF, what are the five categories of security attacks?

Answer

Passive, Active, Close-in, Insider, Distribution.

→ Classification of Attacks Question

What distinguishes passive attacks from active attacks?

Answer

Passive attacks only intercept/monitor traffic without tampering — hard to detect. Active attacks tamper with or disrupt data in transit — detectable because they actively send traffic.

→ Classification of Attacks Question

What are examples of passive attacks?

Answer

Footprinting, sniffing, eavesdropping, network traffic analysis, decryption of weakly encrypted traffic.

→ Classification of Attacks Question

What are examples of active attacks?

Answer

DoS, MitM, session hijacking, spoofing, replay attacks, SQL injection, XSS, malware, privilege escalation, DNS/ARP poisoning, cryptography attacks.

→ Classification of Attacks Question

What is a close-in attack and what examples does it include?

Answer

Attacker in physical proximity gathers, modifies, or disrupts access to information. Examples: shoulder surfing, eavesdropping, dumpster diving.

→ Classification of Attacks Question

What is an insider attack and why is it dangerous?

Answer

Performed by trusted insiders with privileged/physical access who misuse it to violate CIA. Difficult to detect. Examples: data theft, wiretapping, pod slurping, planting keyloggers or backdoors.

→ Classification of Attacks Question

What is a distribution attack?

Answer

Hardware or software tampered with at its source or during transit, before installation. Example: backdoors inserted by vendors at manufacture or during distribution.

→ Classification of Attacks Question

What is information warfare (InfoWar)?

Answer

The use of ICT to gain competitive advantages over an opponent. Weapons include viruses, worms, Trojans, logic bombs, electronic jamming, and penetration tools.

→ Information Warfare Question

Name Libicki's seven categories of information warfare.

Answer

Command & Control (C2), Intelligence-based, Electronic, Psychological, Hacker, Economic, Cyberwarfare.

→ Categories (Libicki) Question

What is cyberwarfare and what makes it the broadest InfoWar category?

Answer

Use of information systems against virtual personas. Includes information terrorism, semantic attacks (taking over systems while appearing normal), and simula-warfare.

→ Categories (Libicki) Question

Distinguish defensive vs. offensive information warfare.

Answer

Defensive: strategies to defend ICT assets (prevention, detection, response). Offensive: attacks against an opponent's ICT assets (web app attacks, malware, MitM, system hacking).

→ Defensive vs. Offensive Question

Who is a hacker?

Answer

An intelligent individual with excellent computer skills who can create and explore software and hardware. Typically a skilled engineer or programmer who discovers vulnerabilities and breaks into systems without authorization.

→ Who is a Hacker? Question

What range of intentions can hackers have?

Answer

From gaining knowledge or treating hacking as a hobby, to illegal activities and malicious acts such as stealing business data, credit card numbers, social security numbers, and email passwords.

→ Who is a Hacker? Question

What is the definition of hacking in computer security?

Answer

Exploiting system vulnerabilities and compromising security controls to gain unauthorized or inappropriate access to a system's resources.

→ What is Hacking? Question

What is the second dimension of hacking beyond exploiting vulnerabilities?

Answer

Modifying system or application features to achieve a goal outside the creator's original purpose.

→ What is Hacking? Question

Name six common network hacking techniques.

Answer

Creating viruses/worms, DoS attacks, trojans/backdoors for unauthorized remote access, botnets, packet sniffing, phishing, password cracking.

→ Common Network Hacking Techniques Question

What are common motives behind hacking?

Answer

Financial gain, information theft, thrill/curiosity, intellectual challenge, prestige, power, peer recognition, vengeance, and experimentation.

→ Motives Behind Hacking Question

What are Script Kiddies and how do they differ from skilled hackers?

Answer

Unskilled hackers who run scripts/tools created by others. Focus on quantity over quality, have no specific target, and aim for popularity or recognition.

→ Hacker Classes Question

What distinguishes White Hat from Black Hat hackers?

Answer

White Hat: cybersecurity professionals who hack defensively with the system owner's permission. Black Hat: use skills for illegal/malicious purposes without authorization; also called crackers.

→ Hacker Classes Question

What are Gray Hat hackers?

Answer

Hackers who operate both offensively and defensively. They may discover vulnerabilities without permission, but sometimes report them to vendors to improve security.

→ Hacker Classes Question

What is a Hacktivist and what are their typical targets?

Answer

Hackers motivated by political or social causes. Typical activities: DDoS, website defacing, data leaks. Targets: government agencies, financial institutions, corporations. Unauthorized access remains a crime regardless of motive.

→ Hacker Classes Question

How do State-Sponsored Hackers differ from Cyber Terrorists?

Answer

State-Sponsored: employed by governments for espionage, intelligence gathering, and infrastructure sabotage against other nations. Cyber Terrorists: extremists motivated by religious/political beliefs, aiming to spread fear via attacks on critical infrastructure.

→ Hacker Classes Question

What are Corporate (Industrial) Spies and what techniques do they use?

Answer

Individuals hired to steal competitor intelligence (blueprints, trade secrets, marketing plans). Use APTs to stay undetected for years and may employ social engineering.

→ Hacker Classes Question

Distinguish Blue Hat, Red Hat, and Green Hat hackers.

Answer

Blue Hat: contract professionals testing systems before release. Red Hat: vigilantes who aggressively target and dismantle black hat operations (not bound by ethical rules). Green Hat: newcomers learning hacking skills, typically in online communities.

→ Hacker Classes Question

What are Insider threats and what makes them dangerous?

Answer

Trusted employees who misuse privileged/physical access to harm the organization. Dangerous because they can bypass security controls. Common sources: disgruntled, terminated, or undertrained employees.

→ Hacker Classes Question

What are Suicide Hackers?

Answer

Hackers who target critical infrastructure for a cause and are unconcerned with legal consequences or punishment — analogous to suicide bombers.

→ Hacker Classes Question

How do Organized Hackers differ from Criminal Syndicates?

Answer

Organized Hackers: hierarchical criminal groups using rented devices/botnets; focus on financial theft and IP/trade-secret theft. Criminal Syndicates: broader criminal organizations exploiting victims across jurisdictions through sophisticated cyber-attacks and money laundering.

→ Hacker Classes Question

What is ethical hacking?

Answer

The practice of using hacking tools, tricks, and techniques to identify vulnerabilities and test network security — performed with the owner's permission and without intent to cause harm.

→ Ethical Hacking Concepts Question

What is the key distinction between an ethical hacker and a cracker?

Answer

Consent. Crackers attempt unauthorized access and conceal activities. Ethical hackers operate with full permission and are completely transparent — making ethical hacking always legal.

→ Ethical Hackers vs. Crackers Question

Define the four key hacking terms: hacker (noun), to hack (verb), cracker/attacker, ethical hacker.

Answer

Hacker: enjoys learning system details and stretching capabilities. To hack: rapid development or reverse engineering to improve software. Cracker/Attacker: uses skills for offensive/illegal purposes. Ethical hacker: uses skills for defensive purposes.

→ Key Terminology Question

Why are vulnerability testing and security audits alone insufficient for network security?

Answer

Hacking requires creative thinking that audits cannot replicate. Organizations must adopt a defense-in-depth strategy by penetrating their own networks to expose vulnerabilities before attackers do.

→ Why Ethical Hacking Is Necessary Question

Name six reasons organizations recruit ethical hackers.

Answer

1. Prevent unauthorized access. 2. Uncover vulnerabilities. 3. Strengthen security posture. 4. Provide preventive measures against breaches. 5. Safeguard customer data. 6. Enhance security awareness at all levels.

→ Why Ethical Hacking Is Necessary Question

What are the three questions an ethical hacker must answer during an assessment?

Answer

1. What can an attacker see on the target? 2. What can an intruder do with that information? 3. Are the attackers' attempts being noticed?

→ Why Ethical Hacking Is Necessary Question

What is the scope of ethical hacking in an organizational context?

Answer

A structured security assessment (pen test or audit) used for risk assessment, auditing, counter fraud, and security best practices. It identifies risks, highlights remedial actions, and reduces ICT costs by resolving vulnerabilities.

→ Scope and Limitations Question

What is a Tiger Team?

Answer

A group of ethical hackers who work together to perform a full-scale security test covering all aspects of the network, as well as physical and system intrusion.

→ Scope and Limitations Question

What three rules must an ethical hacker follow before and during an assessment?

Answer

1. Gain written authorization (signed legal document). 2. Maintain confidentiality via NDA — never disclose test details or sensitive data to third parties. 3. Stay within agreed limits — do not exceed the defined scope.

→ Scope and Limitations Question

What are the six steps of the ethical hacking security audit framework?

Answer

1. Discuss client needs / define scope. 2. Sign NDA. 3. Organize team and schedule. 4. Conduct the test. 5. Analyze results and prepare report. 6. Present findings to the client.

→ Scope and Limitations Question

What are the two limitations of ethical hacking?

Answer

1. The organization must know what they want to find before hiring an outside vendor — otherwise the engagement yields little value. 2. The ethical hacker can only help the organization understand its security; placing the right safeguards remains the organization's responsibility.

→ Scope and Limitations Question

Name the five technical skills of an ethical hacker.

Answer

1. In-depth knowledge of major OSes (Windows, Unix, Linux, Macintosh). 2. In-depth networking knowledge. 3. Expert-level technical proficiency. 4. Knowledge of security areas and issues. 5. High technical knowledge for launching sophisticated attacks.

→ Skills of an Ethical Hacker Question

Name the four non-technical skills of an ethical hacker.

Answer

1. Ability to learn and adapt new technologies quickly. 2. Strong work ethic and problem-solving/communication skills. 3. Commitment to the organization's security policies. 4. Awareness of local standards and laws.

→ Skills of an Ethical Hacker Question

What is AI-driven ethical hacking?

Answer

A modern cybersecurity approach that uses AI technologies — algorithms, machine learning models, and automation frameworks — to enhance ethical hackers' capabilities, anticipate threats, and proactively mitigate risks.

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

What are the four benefits of using AI in ethical hacking?

Answer

Efficiency — faster data processing. Accuracy — fewer human errors. Scalability — handles growing threat complexity. Cost-Effectiveness — automation reduces overall costs.

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

Name the five application domains of AI-driven ethical hacking.

Answer

Network Security, Application Security, Cloud Security, IoT Security, Threat Intelligence.

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

Name the 10 ways AI-driven ethical hacking helps ethical hackers.

Answer

1. Automation of Repetitive Tasks 2. Predictive Analysis 3. Advanced Threat Detection 4. Enhanced Decision Making 5. Adaptive Learning 6. Enhanced Reporting 7. Simulation and Testing 8. Scalability 9. Continuous Monitoring 10. Adaptive Defense Mechanisms

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

How does AI enable Advanced Threat Detection in ethical hacking?

Answer

Using deep learning and anomaly-detection techniques to identify zero-day vulnerabilities and subtle indicators of compromise that traditional methods miss.

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

Distinguish: Predictive Analysis vs. Adaptive Learning in AI-driven ethical hacking.

Answer

Predictive Analysis: uses ML to analyze past attack data and predict future threats before they occur — proactive, forward-looking. Adaptive Learning: continuously updates the AI's knowledge base as new attack types emerge — reactive evolution without manual intervention.

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

Distinguish: Simulation and Testing vs. Continuous Monitoring in AI-driven ethical hacking.

Answer

Simulation and Testing: simulates real-world attacks at a point in time to test defensive resilience and find weaknesses. Continuous Monitoring: always-on real-time assessment of the security posture — identifies and mitigates vulnerabilities as they arise, not just during scheduled tests.

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

Distinguish: Adaptive Learning vs. Adaptive Defense Mechanisms in AI-driven ethical hacking.

Answer

Adaptive Learning: the AI improves its knowledge base and detection strategies over time as new attack types appear. Adaptive Defense Mechanisms: the system updates its algorithms and active response strategies to counteract the latest hacking techniques in operation.

→ AI-Driven Ethical Hacking Question

Why will AI not replace ethical hackers?

Answer

Ethical hacking requires creativity, critical thinking, domain knowledge, and ethical judgment that AI cannot replicate. AI automates routine tasks, but human oversight is essential to interpret results, validate findings, and craft tailored mitigation strategies.

→ Myth: AI Will Replace Ethical Hackers Question

What is the ideal relationship between AI and ethical hackers?

Collaboration: AI provides automation and efficiency; humans provide creativity, contextual judgment, and ethical reasoning. Together they strengthen cybersecurity better than either could alone.

What are the three key features of ChatGPT-powered AI tools for ethical hackers?

Answer

Real-Time Assistance & Task Automation — automates scanning, threat analysis, and reporting via NLP/ML. 3. Threat Intelligence Integration — provides context on identified threats from intelligence databases.

What are the three application benefits of ChatGPT-powered ethical hacking tools?

Answer

Enhanced Security Posture — efficient threat identification and mitigation. Operational Efficiency — automation enables more comprehensive assessments faster. Improved Decision-Making — threat intelligence integration helps prioritize vulnerabilities effectively.

What are the five phases of the CEH Ethical Hacking Framework in order?

Answer

1. Reconnaissance 2. Vulnerability Scanning 3. Gaining Access 4. Maintaining Access 5. Clearing Tracks

→ CEH Framework – Five Phases Question

What is the key difference between an attacker and an ethical hacker in the CEH framework?

Answer

Goals and authorization — not methods. Both follow the same process; ethical hackers have permission and operate with defensive intent.

→ CEH Ethical Hacking Framework Question

Distinguish passive vs. active reconnaissance.

Answer

Passive: no direct interaction — uses public sources, news releases, open-source data. Active: direct interaction — uses tools to detect open ports, hosts, routers, network maps, OSes, and applications.

→ Phase 1: Reconnaissance Question

What is the difference between scanning and enumeration within Phase 1?

Answer

Scanning: identifies active hosts, open ports, and unnecessary services — deeper probing than passive recon. Enumeration: active connections/direct queries to extract user lists, routing tables, shared resources, banners, and security flaws.

→ Phase 1: Reconnaissance Question

What is the goal of Phase 2: Vulnerability Scanning?

Answer

Recognize, measure, and classify security vulnerabilities in systems, networks, and communication channels. Identified vulnerabilities guide further exploitation planning.

→ Phase 2: Vulnerability Scanning Question

What happens during Phase 3: Gaining Access, and what determines success?

Answer

Actual hacking occurs — exploiting vulnerabilities (e.g., password cracking, buffer overflows) for OS- or application-level access. Success depends on target architecture/configuration, attacker skill level, and initial access level obtained.

→ Phase 3: Gaining Access Question

What is privilege escalation and when does it occur?

Answer

After gaining low-privilege access in Phase 3, an attacker exploits known vulnerabilities to raise their privileges to administrator/root level — enabling protected system operations and lateral movement.

→ Phase 3: Gaining Access Question

What four actions does an attacker take in Phase 4: Maintaining Access?

Answer

1. Use the compromised system as a launchpad for further attacks. 2. Upload/download/manipulate data, apps, and configs. 3. Deploy malware to harvest credentials. 4. Close existing vulnerabilities to prevent competing attackers from disrupting their access.

→ Phase 4: Maintaining Access Question

How do attackers clear tracks in Phase 5, and why?

Answer

To remain undetected, attackers modify or delete system logs using log-wiping utilities and remove indicators of compromise. This prevents forensic investigation and extends their undetected presence.

→ Phase 5: Clearing Tracks Question

Name the eight Ethical Hacking Domains in the CEH framework.

Answer

System Hacking, Web App Hacking, Network Hacking, Mobile Hacking, Wireless Hacking, OT/IoT Hacking, Cloud Hacking, Hacking AI.

What is the Cyber Kill Chain methodology and who developed it?

Answer

A component of intelligence-driven defense developed by Lockheed Martin for the identification and prevention of malicious intrusion activities. It describes seven sequential attack phases to help defenders understand adversary TTPs and intervene before the attack succeeds.

→ Cyber Kill Chain Methodology Question

Name the seven phases of the Cyber Kill Chain in order.

Answer

1. Reconnaissance 2. Weaponization 3. Delivery 4. Exploitation 5. Installation 6. Command and Control (C2) 7. Actions on Objectives

→ Cyber Kill Chain Methodology Question

What does an attacker do during Reconnaissance in the Kill Chain?

Answer

Collects public information (Whois, DNS, social networks, open ports, credentials) to identify weak points and potential entry paths before launching an attack.

→ Kill Chain Phase Details Question

What is Weaponization in the Cyber Kill Chain?

Answer

Analyzing reconnaissance data to select or create a tailored malicious payload (e.g., phishing email with a backdoor, exploit kit) targeting identified vulnerabilities — before any delivery to the victim.

→ Kill Chain Phase Details Question

What is the Delivery phase of the Cyber Kill Chain and why is it a key measurement point?

Answer

The payload is transmitted via phishing email, USB, watering hole, or web exploit. It measures the effectiveness of the target's defenses — whether the intrusion attempt is blocked or not.

→ Kill Chain Phase Details Question

Distinguish: Installation vs. Command and Control in the Kill Chain.

Answer

Installation: deploys malware/backdoor on the victim system for persistent access and lateral spread — hidden via encryption. C2: establishes an encrypted two-way channel to the attacker's server for remote control, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration.

→ Kill Chain Phase Details Question

What does an attacker accomplish in Actions on Objectives (Cyber Kill Chain)?

Answer

Achieves intended goals: data theft, service disruption, operational sabotage, or using the compromised system as a launchpad for further attacks.

→ Kill Chain Phase Details Question

Distinguish: Tactics vs. Techniques vs. Procedures (TTPs) in the context of threat actors.

Answer

Tactics: overall strategy across all attack phases (how the actor operates). Techniques: specific technical methods to achieve intermediate results at each stage. Procedures: ordered sequence of actions executing a technique — more actions = higher success + lower detection.

→ TTPs Question

How are Tactics used to profile APT groups?

Answer

By analyzing how they gather info (open-source vs. social engineering), how they approach targets (individual vs. group), and their C2 infrastructure (static vs. dynamic). Early-stage tactics reveal the initial profile; later-stage tactics reveal the full campaign picture.

→ TTPs – Tactics Question

Why are Procedures useful in forensic investigations?

Answer

Different threat actors often implement the same features using the same procedure (e.g., malware self-decryption → evasion → persistence → C2). This commonality allows forensic analysts to identify and attribute threat actors across incidents.

→ TTPs – Procedures Question

What is Adversary Behavioral Identification?

Answer

The identification of common methods and techniques attackers use to penetrate networks. It gives defenders insight into upcoming threats and enables proactive hardening of network security infrastructure.

→ Adversary Behavioral Identification Question

Name the nine adversary behaviors used for detection.

Answer

1. Internal Reconnaissance 2. Use of PowerShell 3. Unspecified Proxy Activities 4. Use of Command-Line Interface 5. HTTP User Agent manipulation 6. Command and Control Server 7. DNS Tunneling 8. Use of Web Shell 9. Data Staging

→ Adversary Behavioral Identification Question

What is an Indicator of Compromise (IoC)?

Answer

Clues, artifacts, and forensic data found on a network or OS indicating a potential intrusion or malicious activity. IoCs are not intelligence themselves — they are data points that feed the intelligence process.

→ Indicators of Compromise Question

Distinguish the three types of IoCs: atomic, computed, and behavioral.

Answer

Atomic: indivisible indicators whose meaning is unchanged in intrusion context (e.g., IP/email addresses). Computed: derived from incident data (e.g., hash values, regex). Behavioral: grouping of atomic + computed indicators combined by logic (e.g., code injection chain).

→ IoC Types Question

What are the four categories of IoCs and what does each cover?

Answer

Email: sender address, subject, attachments/links. Network: URLs, domain names, IP addresses (C2, malware delivery). Host-Based: filenames, hashes, registry keys, DLLs, mutex. Behavioral: specific malicious behaviors, e.g., PowerShell from document, remote command execution.

→ IoC Categories Question

Name six key IoC signals that indicate a potential compromise.

Answer

Unusual outbound network traffic, privileged account anomalies, geographical anomalies, multiple login failures, unusual DNS requests, mismatched port-application traffic. (Also: large HTML response size, DDoS signs, suspicious registry changes, data bundles in wrong places.)

→ Key IoC Signals Question

What is MITRE ATT&CK and what is its purpose?

Answer

A globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. It serves as the foundation for developing threat models and methodologies in the private sector, government, and cybersecurity communities.

→ MITRE ATT&CK Framework Question

What are the three MITRE ATT&CK collections?

Answer

PRE-ATT&CK — reconnaissance, resource development, delivery. ATT&CK for Enterprise — 14 tactics covering initial access through impact. Mobile — iOS and Android-specific tactics and techniques.

→ MITRE ATT&CK Collections Question

How do the 14 Enterprise ATT&CK tactics relate to the Cyber Kill Chain?

Answer

The 14 tactics are derived from the later stages (exploit, control, maintain, execute) of the seven-stage Cyber Kill Chain. This provides finer granularity in describing what can occur during an intrusion after initial compromise.

→ Enterprise ATT&CK Tactics Question

Name the 14 Enterprise ATT&CK tactics in order.

Answer

Reconnaissance, Resource Development, Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Command and Control, Exfiltration, Impact.

→ Enterprise ATT&CK Tactics Question

What are three use cases of MITRE ATT&CK?

Answer

1. Prioritize development of network defense capabilities. 2. Determine coverage of defense capabilities against known threats. 3. Identify commonalities between threat actors and describe intrusion chains with a common reference.

→ MITRE ATT&CK Use Cases Question

What is the Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis and what is the Diamond event?

Answer

A framework for identifying clusters of events correlated across an organization's systems. The Diamond event is the vital atomic element of any intrusion — consisting of four core features: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, and Victim, arranged in a diamond shape.

→ Diamond Model Question

What are the four core features of the Diamond Model and what key question does each answer?

Answer

Adversary — Who was behind the attack. Victim — Where the attack was performed. Capability — How the attack was carried out. Infrastructure — What the adversary used to reach the victim.

→ Diamond Model – Core Features Question

Name the six event meta-features of the Diamond Model.

Answer

Timestamp, Phase, Result, Direction, Methodology, Resource.

→ Diamond Model – Meta-Features Question

What two meta-features does the Extended Diamond Model add, and what do they describe?

Answer

Socio-Political — describes the relationship/motivation between Adversary and Victim (e.g., financial gain, espionage, hacktivism). Technology — describes how technology enables Infrastructure and Capability for communication and operation.

→ Extended Diamond Model Question

What does the Result meta-feature represent in the Diamond Model?

Answer

The outcome of the event: success, failure, or unknown. Can also be classified using CIA: Confidentiality compromised, Integrity compromised, or Availability compromised.

→ Diamond Model – Meta-Features Question

What is Information Assurance (IA)?

Answer

Assurance of the integrity, availability, confidentiality, and authenticity of information and information systems during usage, processing, storage, and transmission. Achieved through physical, technical, and administrative controls.

→ Information Assurance Question

What do Information Assurance (IA) and Information Risk Management (IRM) ensure?

Answer

That only authorized personnel access and use information. Together they achieve information security and business continuity.

→ Information Assurance Question

Name all eight Information Assurance processes in order.

Answer

1. Develop local policy, process, and guidance. 2. Design network and user authentication strategies. 3. Identify network vulnerabilities and threats. 4. Identify problems and resource requirements. 5. Create plans for identified resource requirements. 6. Apply appropriate information assurance controls. 7. Perform Certification and Accreditation (C&A). 8. Provide information assurance training.

→ Eight Key IA Processes Question

What is the purpose of designing network and user authentication strategies in IA?

Answer

To secure network infrastructure and protect user credentials, thereby protecting privacy and information on the network.

→ Eight Key IA Processes Question

What role do vulnerability assessments play in the IA process?

Answer

They outline the security posture of the network by identifying vulnerabilities and threats, enabling organizations to implement proper countermeasures.

→ Eight Key IA Processes Question

What does Certification and Accreditation (C&A) accomplish in IA?

Answer

Validates that information systems meet security requirements, traces vulnerabilities, and implements safety measures to nullify them.

→ Eight Key IA Processes Question

Why is information assurance training critical in the IA program?

Answer

It brings awareness of information technology security to all personnel in federal and private organizations, building organizational security culture.

→ Eight Key IA Processes Question

What is Continual/Adaptive Security Strategy?

Answer

A defense approach that prescribes continuous Predict, Protect, Detect, and Respond actions to ensure comprehensive computer network defense. It enables organizations to anticipate threats, prevent compromise, identify intrusions, and remediate incidents in real time.

→ Continual/Adaptive Security Strategy Question

Name the four pillars of adaptive security strategy in order.

Answer

1. Predict 2. Protect 3. Detect 4. Respond

→ Continual/Adaptive Security Strategy Question

What is the purpose of the Predict pillar in adaptive security?

Answer

To identify potential attacks, targets, and methods before they materialize into viable threats. Activities include risk and vulnerability assessments, attack surface analysis, and consumption of threat intelligence data.

→ Continual/Adaptive Security Strategy Question

What is the purpose of the Protect pillar in adaptive security?

Answer

To eliminate vulnerabilities and deploy prior countermeasures that prevent unauthorized access and compromise. Measures include security policies, physical security, host security, firewalls, and intrusion detection systems (IDS).

→ Continual/Adaptive Security Strategy Question

What is the purpose of the Detect pillar in adaptive security?

Answer

To assess the network for abnormalities such as attacks, damages, unauthorized access attempts, and modifications, and locate them. Includes regular monitoring of network traffic using network monitoring and packet sniffing tools.

→ Continual/Adaptive Security Strategy Question

What is the purpose of the Respond pillar in adaptive security?

Answer

To identify incidents, determine root causes, execute containment and eradication, and mitigate impact. Actions include incident response, investigation, impact mitigation, and deciding whether an incident is real or a false positive.

→ Continual/Adaptive Security Strategy Question

What is Defense-in-Depth?

Answer

A security strategy in which multiple protection layers are placed throughout an information system. It applies the military principle that a complex, multi-layered defense system is more difficult to defeat than a single barrier.

→ Defense-in-Depth Question

What are the three key benefits of Defense-in-Depth?

Answer

1. Prevents direct attacks — a break in one layer only leads to the next. 2. Minimizes impact — limits scope and severity of damage if accessed. 3. Provides time for response — gives time to deploy countermeasures before intrusion spreads.

→ Defense-in-Depth Benefits Question

Name the seven layers of Defense-in-Depth.

Answer

1. Policies, Procedures, and Awareness 2. Physical Security 3. Perimeter Security 4. Internal Network 5. Host Security 6. Application Security 7. Data Security

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What is included in the Policies, Procedures, and Awareness layer of Defense-in-Depth?

Answer

Organizational security guidelines, policies, procedures, and user training to establish security culture and behavior standards.

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What does the Physical Security layer of Defense-in-Depth include?

Answer

Access controls, CCTV, locks, and environmental controls to prevent unauthorized physical access to systems and infrastructure.

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What security measures are included in the Perimeter Security layer?

Answer

Firewalls, boundary protection, and network segmentation to control and monitor traffic entering and leaving the network.

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What measures are included in the Internal Network layer of Defense-in-Depth?

Answer

Intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS), network monitoring, and access controls to protect traffic and systems within the network perimeter.

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What is included in the Host Security layer of Defense-in-Depth?

Answer

Operating system hardening, antivirus software, host-based firewalls, and patch management to protect individual systems from compromise.

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What is included in the Application Security layer of Defense-in-Depth?

Answer

Secure coding practices, input validation, and application-level authentication and authorization to prevent exploitation of application vulnerabilities.

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What measures are used for Data Security in Defense-in-Depth?

Answer

Encryption, data classification, access controls, and backup and recovery procedures to protect information at rest and in transit.

→ Defense-in-Depth Layers Question

What is Risk?

Answer

The degree of uncertainty or expectation that an adverse event may cause damage to the system or its resources. It is the combination of the probability of a threat and the consequence or impact of that event.

→ Risk Management Question

What is the formula for calculating Risk?

Answer

Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Impact or Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × Asset Value. Can also be expressed as Level of Risk = Consequence × Likelihood.

→ What is Risk? Question

What is the formula for calculating Level of Risk in the context of Risk Levels?

Answer

Level of Risk = Consequence × Likelihood — where Consequence is the severity of impact and Likelihood is the probability of occurrence.

→ Risk Levels Question

Name the three main risk levels.

Answer

1. Extreme or High (Serious or Imminent danger) 2. Medium (Moderate danger) 3. Low (Negligible danger)

→ Risk Levels Question

What action should be taken for Extreme or High risk?

Answer

Immediate measures are required to combat the risk. Identify and impose controls to reduce risk to a reasonably low level.

→ Risk Levels Question

What action should be taken for Medium risk?

Answer

Immediate action is not required, but action should be implemented quickly. Implement controls as soon as possible to reduce risk to a reasonably low level.

→ Risk Levels Question

What action should be taken for Low risk?

Answer

Take preventive steps to mitigate the effects of risk.

→ Risk Levels Question

What is a Risk Matrix?

Answer

A graphical representation that scales likelihood (probability) against consequences (impact) to visualize and compare risks. It helps organizations prioritize risk remediation efforts based on probability and impact severity.

→ Risk Matrix Question

What are the two key dimensions of a Risk Matrix?

Answer

Likelihood (Probability): The chance that a risk event will occur. Consequence (Impact): The severity or extent of damage if a risk event occurs.

→ Risk Matrix Question

Can control measures completely eliminate risk?

Answer

No. Control measures may decrease the level of risk, but do not always entirely eliminate it. Risk management requires ongoing monitoring and adaptation.

→ Key Risk Concepts Question

What is Risk Management?

Answer

The process of reducing and maintaining risk at an acceptable level by means of a well-defined and actively employed security program. It is continuous and helps organizations identify, assess, respond to, and control potential effects of risk.

→ Risk Management Process Question

Name the five key Risk Management Phases in order.

Answer

1. Risk Identification 2. Risk Assessment 3. Risk Treatment 4. Risk Tracking 5. Risk Review

→ Risk Management Phases Question

What is the main objective of Risk Identification?

Answer

To identify the sources, causes, and consequences of internal and external risks affecting the organization's security before they cause harm. The process depends on skill set and differs by organization.

→ Risk Management Phases Question

What is Risk Assessment and what does it accomplish?

Answer

An ongoing iterative process that assesses the organization's risks and estimates their likelihood and impact. It assigns priorities for mitigation, determines quantitative/qualitative value, and detects and prioritizes risks.

→ Risk Management Phases Question

What is Risk Treatment?

Answer

The process of selecting and implementing appropriate controls on identified risks to modify them based on severity level. Decisions are based on risk assessment results and aim to address risks outside the organization's risk tolerance.

→ Risk Management Phases Question

What is Risk Tracking?

Answer

Continuous monitoring and observation of implemented controls and risk status. Includes monitoring control effectiveness, tracking risk indicators, maintaining risk registers, and observing for emerging risks.

→ Risk Management Phases Question

What is Risk Review?

Answer

Periodic evaluation and assessment of risk management strategies and control effectiveness. Includes reviewing control performance, verifying procedures are understood and followed, and identifying improvement opportunities.

→ Risk Management Phases Question

Name six key considerations before treating a risk.

Answer

1. The appropriate method of treatment 2. People responsible for implementation 3. Costs involved 4. Benefits of treatment 5. Likelihood of success 6. Ways to measure and assess treatment effectiveness

→ Risk Treatment Considerations Question

Define Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI).

Answer

The collection and analysis of information about threats and adversaries, including patterns that enable knowledgeable decisions for preparedness, prevention, and response actions against cyber attacks. CTI converts unknown threats into known threats through research and analysis.

→ Definition Question

What are the four types of threat intelligence?

Answer

1. Strategic 2. Tactical 3. Operational 4. Technical. They differ in data collection, analysis, and consumption based on audience and goals.

→ Types of Threat Intelligence Question

Who consumes Strategic Threat Intelligence and what does it focus on?

Answer

Consumed by: High-level executives, IT management, CISOFocus: Long-term issues, high-level cybersecurity posture, attack trends, financial impact, business decisions

→ Strategic Threat Intelligence Question

What information does Strategic Threat Intelligence include?

Answer

Financial impact of cyber activity, attribution for breaches, threat actors and attack trends, threat landscape by sector, breach and malware statistics, geopolitical conflicts, changes in adversary TTPs, industry impact analysis

→ Strategic Threat Intelligence Question

Who consumes Tactical Threat Intelligence and what does it provide?

Answer

Consumed by: IT service managers, security managers, NOC staff, administratorsProvides: Information on tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by threat actors to perform attacks

→ Tactical Threat Intelligence Question

How do organizations use Tactical Threat Intelligence?

Answer

Develop detection and mitigation strategies, update security products with identified indicators, patch vulnerable systems, assess technical capabilities and goals of attackers, analyze security incidents and assess attack vectors

→ Tactical Threat Intelligence Question

Define Operational Threat Intelligence and who consumes it.

Answer

Information about specific threats against the organization with contextual details about security events and incidents. Consumed by: Security managers, heads of incident response, network defenders, forensics and fraud detection teams

→ Operational Threat Intelligence Question

What sources are used for Operational Threat Intelligence?

Answer

Human intelligence, social media, chat rooms, real-world activities and events that result in cyber attacks. Obtained by analyzing human behavior and threat groups. Typically collected by government organizations.

→ Operational Threat Intelligence Question

What is Technical Threat Intelligence and what does it focus on?

Answer

Information about resources (tools, command and control channels) attackers use to perform attacks. Focuses on: Specific indicators of compromise (IoCs), has shorter lifespan than tactical intelligence, enables rapid distribution and response

→ Technical Threat Intelligence Question

Name examples of Technical Threat Intelligence.

Answer

Specific malware implementations, IP addresses and domains used by malicious endpoints, phishing email headers, hash checksums of malware

→ Technical Threat Intelligence Question

How is Technical Threat Intelligence applied in organizations?

Answer

Added to defensive systems (IDS/IPS, firewalls, endpoint security) to enhance detection mechanisms. Directly fed into security devices in digital format to block and identify inbound and outbound malicious traffic.

→ Technical Threat Intelligence Question

What is the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle and why is it important?

Answer

A continuous process of developing intelligence from raw data that supports organizations in developing defensive mechanisms to thwart emerging risks and threats. Higher-level executives provide continuous feedback at every stage to ensure intelligence relevance and accuracy.

→ Threat Intelligence Lifecycle Question

Name the five phases of the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle in order.

Answer

1. Planning and Direction 2. Collection 3. Processing and Exploitation 4. Analysis and Production 5. Dissemination and Integration

→ Threat Intelligence Lifecycle Question

What is the purpose of the Planning and Direction phase of the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle?

Answer

Develop a proper plan based on strategic intelligence requirements and define the entire intelligence program from data collection to delivery. Forms intelligence team, establishes roles/responsibilities, and sets planning for later cycle phases.

→ Phase 1: Planning and Direction Question

What is the purpose of the Collection phase of the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle?

Answer

Gather desired intelligence from multiple sources using technical and human means. Collect required data that satisfies intelligence goals from HUMINT, IMINT, MASINT, SIGINT, OSINT, IoCs, and third-party sources including critical applications, network infrastructure, and security infrastructure.

→ Phase 2: Collection Question

Name the six main collection methods/sources for threat intelligence.

Answer

1. Human Intelligence (HUMINT) 2. Imagery Intelligence (IMINT) 3. Measurement and Signature Intelligence (MASINT) 4. Signal Intelligence (SIGINT) 5. Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) 6. Indicators of Compromise (IoCs)

→ Phase 2: Collection Question

What is the purpose of the Processing and Exploitation phase of the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle?

Answer

Transform raw data into meaningful, usable information. Convert raw data into useful information using sophisticated technology and tools, highly trained professionals, and automated processing functions (decryption, parsing, filtering, data correlation, aggregation).

→ Phase 3: Processing and Exploitation Question

What is the purpose of the Analysis and Production phase of the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle?

Answer

Analyze processed intelligence to extract refined information and identify threats. Combine information from various sources into a single entity. Apply analysis techniques (qualitative, quantitative, machine-based, statistical) to convert raw data into intelligence and develop appropriate countermeasures to respond to identified threats.

→ Phase 4: Analysis and Production Question

What four characteristics must threat intelligence analysis have?

Answer

Objective: Unbiased and evidence-basedTimely: Delivered when neededAccurate: Correct and verifiedActionable: Can be directly used for decision-making

→ Phase 4: Analysis and Production Question

Name four reasoning techniques used in threat intelligence analysis.

Answer

1. Deduction (general to specific) 2. Induction (specific to general) 3. Abduction (best explanation) 4. Scientific method (confidence-based analysis)

→ Phase 4: Analysis and Production Question

What is the purpose of the Dissemination and Integration phase of the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle?

Answer

Deliver analyzed intelligence to intended consumers at strategic, operational, tactical, and technical levels. Distribute through automated and manual methods. Gather feedback from consumers on intelligence accuracy and relevance. Feedback completes the cycle and provides inputs to refine intelligence requirements for the next iteration.

→ Phase 5: Dissemination and Integration Question

What are the major intelligence information types used for dissemination?

Answer

Threat indicators and Indicators of Compromise (IoCs), Adversary Tactics/Techniques/Procedures (TTPs), security alerts, threat intelligence reports, tool configuration information

→ Phase 5: Dissemination and Integration Question

Who consumes strategic threat intelligence and what is the focus?

Answer

Consumers: High-level executives and managementFocus: Business strategies and risk-based decisions for organizational security posture

→ Phase 5: Dissemination and Integration Question

Who consumes tactical and operational threat intelligence?

Answer

Tactical: IT service and SOC managers, administrators, architects; focus on adversary TTPsOperational: Security managers and network defenders; focus on specific threats to organization

→ Phase 5: Dissemination and Integration Question

What is the purpose of the feedback loop in the Threat Intelligence Lifecycle?

Answer

Consumers provide assessment on whether extracted intelligence meets their requirements. Feedback describes accuracy and relevance. Cycle repeats with refined requirements and methods to produce more accurate, timely, and relevant intelligence.

→ Phase 5: Dissemination and Integration Question

What is Threat Modeling and what is its primary purpose?

Answer

A risk assessment approach for analyzing the security of an application by capturing, organizing, and analyzing all information that affects it. Purpose is to identify relevant threats, key vulnerabilities, and improve security design through comprehensive threat analysis.

→ Threat Modeling Question

What are the three benefits of threat modeling?

Answer

1. Identify relevant threats to a particular application scenario 2. Identify key vulnerabilities in an application's design 3. Improve security design through comprehensive analysis and understanding of threats

→ Purpose and Benefits Question

Name the five steps of the Threat Modeling Process in order.

Answer

1. Identify Security Objectives 2. Application Overview 3. Decompose the Application 4. Identify Threats 5. Identify Vulnerabilities

→ Threat Modeling Process Question

What is the purpose of Step 1: Identify Security Objectives in the Threat Modeling Process?

Answer

Define goals and constraints related to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Guide threat modeling efforts and determine how much effort to put toward subsequent steps. Key questions: What data to protect? Compliance requirements? Quality-of-service requirements? Intangible assets?

→ Step 1: Identify Security Objectives Question

What does Step 2: Application Overview of the Threat Modeling Process involve?

Answer

Understand application structure by identifying components, data flows, trust boundaries. Includes deployment topology, logical layers, key services/components, communication protocols, roles, usage scenarios, technology stack, and security mechanisms.

→ Step 2: Application Overview Question

What is the purpose of Step 3: Decompose the Application in the Threat Modeling Process?

Answer

Break down the application to identify trust boundaries, data flows, entry points, and exit points. Makes it easier to find more relevant and detailed threats and vulnerabilities by understanding application structure and component interactions.

→ Step 3: Decompose the Application Question

How does Step 4: Identify Threats of the Threat Modeling Process work and what approach is used?

Answer

Identify threats relevant to control scenario and context using information from application overview and decomposition. Bring development and test teams together, start with common threats grouped by vulnerability category, and use a question-driven approach.

→ Step 4: Identify Threats Question

What is the purpose of Step 5: Identify Vulnerabilities in the Threat Modeling Process?

Answer

Find weaknesses in the application that allow attacker exploitation and lead to security breaches. Identify weaknesses related to threats found using vulnerability categories and fix them beforehand to prevent breaches.

→ Step 5: Identify Vulnerabilities Question

What are the key elements of a deployment diagram in threat modeling?

Answer

End-to-end deployment topology, logical layers, key components and services, communication ports and protocols, identities, external dependencies, and trust boundaries

→ Application Overview Components Question

What should be included in Application Security Mechanisms review during threat modeling?

Answer

Input/data validation, authorization/authentication, sensitive data handling, configuration management, session management, parameter manipulation, cryptography, exception management, auditing and logging

→ Application Overview Components Question

What are trust boundaries and why are they important in threat modeling?

Answer

Points where trust levels change between different parts of an application. Important because they help administrators focus on relevant areas and identify where extra privileges or specific security controls are needed. Include outer boundaries, access control points, and data flow perspectives.

What is the difference between Entry Points and Exit Points in threat modeling?

Answer

Entry Points: Where users interact with application or internal components communicate; can serve as attack vectors; focus on critical functionalities. Exit Points: Where application transfers data to clients/external systems; prioritize points writing untrusted or client input data.

What is Incident Management and what are its core objectives?

Answer

A set of defined processes to identify, analyze, prioritize, and resolve security incidents to restore normal service operations as quickly as possible. Core objectives include improving service quality, resolving problems proactively, reducing incident impact, meeting availability requirements, and assisting with handling future incidents.

→ Incident Management Question

What five components does incident management involve?

Answer

1. Vulnerability Analysis (identifying exploitable software/systems) 2. Artifact Analysis (examining forensic evidence) 3. Security Awareness Training (helping users recognize suspicious events) 4. Intrusion Detection (monitoring unauthorized access) 5. Public/Technology Monitoring (tracking security announcements)

→ What Incident Management Involves Question

What are the objectives of the incident management process?

Answer

1. Improve service quality 2. Resolve problems proactively 3. Reduce the impact of incidents on the organization or its business operations 4. Meet service availability requirements 5. Increase staff efficiency and productivity 6. Improve user and customer satisfaction 7. Assist in handling future incidents

What role do Human Resources personnel play in incident management?

Answer

Take steps to terminate or remove employees suspected of harmful computer activities or security violations. Respond to insider threats and malicious employee behavior identified through incident investigation.

What is the responsibility of Legal Counsel in incident management?

Answer

Set rules and regulations for the organization, influence internal security policies and practices, provide legal guidance on compliance and implications of incidents, and advise on handling of insider threats or external attacks involving harmful or malicious activities.
