docs.title: Overview
docs.text: DNS footprinting is the phase in the footprinting methodology that follows Whois footprinting. Attackers query DNS infrastructure to collect information about DNS servers, DNS records, and the types of servers used by the target organization.

docs.title: Purpose and Attacker Value
docs.text: The data gathered enables attackers to identify hosts connected to the target network and provides a foundation for deeper exploitation of the target organization.

docs.title: Key Techniques
docs.text:
• DNS record extraction — querying DNS servers for various record types to enumerate the target's infrastructure
  • Reverse DNS lookups — resolving IP addresses back to hostnames to map the network
  • DNS interrogation tools — automated tools that systematically query DNS servers to extract records at scale

docs.title: Extracting DNS Information
docs.text: DNS footprinting reveals DNS zone data, which includes DNS domain names, computer names, IP addresses, and much more information about a network. An attacker uses DNS information to determine key hosts in the network and then performs social engineering attacks to gather even more information.

docs.title: DNS Record Types
docs.text: Record Type Description A Points to a host's IP address AAAA Points to a host's IPv6 address MX Points to domain's mail server NS Points to host's name server CNAME Canonical naming; allows aliases to a host SOA Indicate authority for a domain SRV Service records PTR Maps IP address to a hostname RP Responsible person HINFO Host information record; includes CPU type and OS TXT Unstructured text records

docs.title: DNS Interrogation Tools
docs.text:
Attackers use DNS interrogation tools such as SecurityTrails, Fierce, DNSChecker, zdns, and DNSdumpster.com to perform DNS footprinting. These tools can extract a range of IP addresses using IP routing lookup. If the target network allows unknown, unauthorized users to transfer DNS zone data, it is easy for an attacker to obtain DNS information with the help of a DNS interrogation tool.

When an attacker queries a DNS server using a DNS interrogation tool, the server responds with a record structure that contains information about the target DNS. DNS records provide important information regarding the locations and types of servers.

docs.title: SecurityTrails
docs.text:
Source: https://securitytrails.com

SecurityTrails is an advanced DNS enumeration tool capable of creating a DNS map of the target domain network. It can enumerate both current and historical DNS records such as A, AAAA, NS, MX, SOA, and TXT, which helps in building the DNS structure. It also enumerates all existing subdomains of the target domain using brute-force techniques.

docs.title: Fierce
docs.text:
Source: https://github.com/mschwager/fierce

Fierce is a DNS reconnaissance tool used for scanning and collecting crucial information about the target domain. Attackers can use it to enumerate subdomains, identify non-contiguous IP spaces, and find hostnames linked with specified domains or subdomains. This helps attackers create a network environment map and identify potential targets for exploitation.

Command Purpose fierce --domain certifiedhacker.com Basic scan with no additional options fierce --domain certifiedhacker.com --subdomains write admin mail Scan for specific subdomains (e.g., write, admin, mail) fierce --domain certifiedhacker.com --subdomains mail --traverse 10 Scan domains near discovered records; --traverse 10 searches contiguous IP blocks within a range of 10 fierce --domain certifiedhacker.com --subdomains mail --connect Attempt HTTP connection on discovered domains fierce --domain certifiedhacker.com --wide Full detailed scan of all discovered records

docs.title: DNS Lookup with AI
docs.text:
Attackers can leverage AI-powered technologies to enhance and automate their footprinting tasks. With the aid of AI, attackers can effortlessly perform reverse DNS lookup activities on a target and acquire valuable insights.

For example, attackers can use ChatGPT with a prompt such as:

"Install and use DNSRecon to perform DNS enumeration on the target domain www.certifiedhacker.com"

The following shell command is generated to perform DNS enumeration using the dnsrecon tool:

sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y dnsrecon && dnsrecon -d certifiedhacker.com -t std
Command Part Explanation sudo apt-get update Updates the package lists for upgrades and new package installations && Concatenates commands to execute them sequentially sudo apt-get install -y dnsrecon Installs the dnsrecon tool with automatic "yes" to all prompts dnsrecon -d certifiedhacker.com -t std Initiates dnsrecon to perform DNS enumeration on the target domain using standard enumeration techniques

docs.title: Reverse DNS Lookup
docs.text:
DNS lookup finds the IP address for a given domain name; a reverse DNS operation obtains the domain name of a given IP address. When a domain name is entered in a browser, DNS converts it into an IP address using a record and forwards the request for further processing. Attackers perform a reverse DNS lookup on an IP range to locate a DNS PTR record for those IP addresses.

Attackers use various tools such as DNSRecon, Reverse Lookup, puredns, Reverse IP Domain Check, and Reverse IP Lookup to perform reverse DNS lookup on the target host. When an IP address or range is obtained, these tools can resolve it back to a domain name.

docs.title: DNSRecon
docs.text:
Source: https://github.com/darkoperator/dnsrecon

Command to perform a reverse DNS lookup on a range of IP addresses:

dnsrecon -r 162.241.216.0-162.241.216.255

The -r option specifies the range of IP addresses (first to last) for a reverse lookup by brute force.

docs.title: Reverse Lookup
docs.text:
Source: https://mxtoolbox.com

The Reverse Lookup tool performs a reverse IP lookup by taking an IP address and locating a DNS PTR record for that IP address.

docs.title: Flashcards – Module 02
docs.text:
Question

What is reconnaissance/footprinting?

Answer

The preparatory phase where an attacker gathers as much information as possible about a target prior to launching an attack. It is the first step in ethical hacking and results in a blueprint (unique system profile) of the target.

→ Footprinting Concepts Question

What is the difference between passive and active footprinting?

Answer

Passive: No direct interaction; hard to detect; uses OSINT, search engines, databases.Active: Direct interaction with the target; may be detected; includes DNS interrogation, port scanning, social engineering.

→ Types of Footprinting Question

Name three techniques used in passive footprinting.

Answer

1. Open-source Intelligence (OSINT) gathering2. Proprietary databases and paid services3. Sharing intelligence with partner organizations or industry groups

→ Passive Footprinting Question

Name four techniques used in active footprinting.

Answer

1. DNS interrogation2. Social engineering3. Network/port scanning4. User and service enumeration

→ Active Footprinting Question

What three categories of information are gathered during footprinting?

Answer

Organization: employee details, locations, web technologies, press releases.Network: domains, network blocks, IP addresses, DNS/Whois records.System: web server OS, server locations, email addresses, credentials.

→ Information Obtained in Footprinting Question

Name six threats enabled by footprinting.

Answer

1. Social Engineering2. System and Network Attacks3. Information Leakage4. Privacy Loss5. Corporate Espionage6. Business Loss

→ Footprinting Threats Question

Name six techniques used in the footprinting methodology.

Answer

1. Search Engines (Google hacking, SHODAN)2. Internet Research Services (people search, archive.org, dark web)3. Social Networking Sites4. Whois Footprinting5. DNS Footprinting6. Network & Email Footprinting+ Social Engineering (eavesdropping, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving, impersonation)

→ Footprinting Methodology Question

What is Google hacking?

Answer

The use of advanced Google search operators to create complex queries that extract sensitive or hidden information and identify vulnerable targets.

→ Advanced Google Hacking Question

What is the Google Hacking Database (GHDB)?

Answer

A curated database of Google hacking queries used to identify sensitive data such as login portals, error messages, vulnerable web apps, and exposed files on public servers.

→ Advanced Google Hacking Question

What is the correct syntax for a Google advanced search operator?

Answer

operator:search_term — no space between the operator and the query term.

→ Operator Syntax Question

What is the difference between inurl: and allinurl:?

Answer

inurl: requires one specified term in the URL. allinurl: requires all query terms to appear in the URL.

→ Search Operators Question

What does the cache: operator return?

Answer

Google's cached (stored) version of a web page, not the current live version. Useful for viewing deleted or changed content.

→ Search Operators Question

What does the site: operator do?

Answer

Restricts search results to a specified site or domain.Example: games site:certifiedhacker.com

→ Search Operators Question

What does the intext: operator do?

Answer

Returns pages containing the specified keyword in the body of the webpage.Example: intext:"vpn configuration"

→ Search Operators Question

What is the difference between intitle: and allintitle:?

Answer

intitle: requires one term in the page title (other terms match anywhere). allintitle: requires all query terms to appear in the title.Example: malware detection intitle:help vs allintitle: detect malware

→ Search Operators Question

What is the difference between inanchor: and allinanchor:?

Answer

inanchor: requires one term in the anchor text of inbound links. allinanchor: requires all terms in the anchor text.Example: Anti-virus inanchor:Norton

→ Search Operators Question

What does the link: operator do?

Answer

Finds pages that contain links pointing to the specified URL.Example: link:www.googleguide.com

→ Search Operators Question

What does the related: operator do?

Answer

Displays websites that are similar or related to the specified URL.Example: related:www.microsoft.com

→ Search Operators Question

What does the info: operator do?

Answer

Presents information that Google has about a specific web page.Example: info:gothotel.com

→ Search Operators Question

What does the location: operator do?

Answer

Returns results for a specific geographic location.Example: location: 4 seasons restaurant

→ Search Operators Question

What does the filetype: operator do?

Answer

Filters results by file extension.Example: jasmine filetype:jpg returns JPG files related to "jasmine."

→ Search Operators Question

What does the source: operator do?

Answer

Returns results from a specific source in Google News.Example: Malware news source:"Hacker News"

→ Search Operators Question

What does the phonebook: operator do?

Answer

Finds residential and business phone numbers for a person or organization.Example: phonebook:Sundar Pichai

→ Search Operators Question

What is the difference between before: and after:?

Answer

before:YYYY-MM-DD filters results to content published before the date. after:YYYY-MM-DD filters to content published after the date.Example: ransomware before:2020-06-29

→ Search Operators Question

Name five types of sensitive data an attacker can find using GHDB queries.

Answer

1. Files containing passwords2. Login/logon portals3. Firewall/IDS logs and configurations4. Software version information5. Hidden intranet/VPN pages

→ GHDB Extractions Question

What is the GHDB and where is it hosted?

Answer

The Google Hacking Database is a subset of the Exploit-DB, hosting Google Dork queries that uncover sensitive information inadvertently exposed on the web.

→ GHDB Question

Name the 14 GHDB categories.

Answer

Footholds · Files Containing Usernames · Sensitive Directories · Web Server Detection · Vulnerable Files · Vulnerable Servers · Error Messages · Files Containing Juicy Info · Files Containing Passwords · Sensitive Online Shopping Info · Network or Vulnerability Data · Pages Containing Login Portals · Various Online Devices · Advisories and Vulnerabilities

→ GHDB Categories Question

Name five ways attackers leverage the GHDB.

Answer

1. Reconnaissance — gather info on exposed files and devices2. Exploiting Misconfigurations — unauthorized access via misconfigured servers3. Finding Vulnerable Systems — locate outdated software4. Credential Harvesting — extract usernames/passwords5. Identifying Open Ports and Services — map entry points

→ How Attackers Leverage the GHDB Question

What is SearchSploit and when is it useful?

Answer

A command-line tool for Exploit-DB that enables offline searching of a locally checked-out copy of the exploit repository. Especially useful for assessments on air-gapped or segregated networks without Internet access.

→ SearchSploit Question

What type of information do Google dorks reveal when used for VPN footprinting?

Answer

Login portals, VPN key directories, server configurations, and specific VPN product login pages (e.g., Fortinet, Cisco ASA, Zyxel, Citrix Gateway, OpenVPN).

→ VPN Footprinting through GHDB Question

What makes Shodan different from traditional search engines, and what does it index?

Answer

Shodan indexes internet-connected devices and services (not web content), exposing open ports, service banners, and device configurations. Used to detect vulnerable devices and networks, including VoIP and VPN systems.

→ SHODAN Question

What footprinting information can Google Advanced Search reveal that a normal search cannot?

Answer

Sites linking back to the target — revealing partners, vendors, clients, and affiliations. Enables complex condition-based queries without typing operators.

→ Google Advanced Search Question

What is reverse image search and how do attackers use it?

Answer

Uses an image (uploaded or via URL) as the search query to find all online locations of that image. Attackers use it to track profile pictures, photos, and location details of a target.Tools: Google, TinEye, Bing, Yahoo, Pinterest.

→ Reverse Image Search Question

What hidden information can attackers extract from videos using analysis tools?

Answer

Upload time/date, thumbnails, geolocation metadata, and other embedded data. Tools: YouTube Metadata, YouTube DataViewer, MW Metadata, EZGif, VideoReverser.com.

→ Video Search Engines Question

What is a meta search engine and what advantage does it offer over regular search engines?

Answer

A meta search engine has no own index — it simultaneously queries multiple search engines (Google, Bing, Ask.com), aggregates and de-duplicates results. Returns broader results with less effort and hides the user's IP address.Examples: Startpage, MetaGer, eTools.ch.

→ Meta Search Engines Question

What do FTP search engines index and what can attackers find through them?

Answer

FTP search engines index files on FTP servers — many left unsecured and accessible via browser. Attackers can find business strategies, financial records, employee records, tax documents, and licensed software.Examples: NAPALM FTP Indexer, FreewareWeb FTP File Search, Mamont, Globalfilesearch.com.

→ FTP Search Engines Question

What are IoT search engines and what devices can attackers discover through them?

Answer

IoT search engines crawl the Internet for publicly accessible IoT devices. Attackers can discover SCADA systems, traffic control systems, CCTV cameras, and industrial/household appliances — many unsecured or using default credentials.Examples: Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye.

→ IoT Search Engines Question

What information can attackers obtain about a target IoT device via IoT search engines?

Answer

Manufacturer details, geographical location, IP address, hostname, and open ports — used to establish back doors and launch further attacks.

→ IoT Search Engines Question

What kind of information does a company's TLD (public website) expose?

Answer

Organizational history, services and products, and contact information. The external URL can be located via search engines such as Google and Bing.

→ TLDs and Sub-domains Question

Why are sub-domains often more vulnerable than the main domain?

Answer

Admins often create sub-domains for testing before production deployment. These remain in a testing/insecure state, making them more susceptible to exploitation.

→ TLDs and Sub-domains Question

What critical information can sub-domain enumeration reveal?

Answer

Departmental structure, source code and documents on webservers, access control mechanisms (IP, domain, subnet, credentials), and private organizational functions.

→ TLDs and Sub-domains Question

What Google advanced search operator is used to find sub-domains while excluding the main www site?

Answer

site:microsoft.com -inurl:www — returns indexed pages under the domain while excluding results containing "www" in the URL.

→ TLDs and Sub-domains Question

What are the three main tools used for sub-domain discovery, and what does each reveal?

Answer

Netcraft: sub-domains, web server OS, hosting provider, SSL data.DNSdumpster: hosts, sub-domains, IP addresses, DNS servers.Pentest-Tools Find Subdomains: sub-domains, IPs, OS, server technology, web platform, page titles.

→ Tools for Sub-domain Discovery Question

How can AI (e.g., ChatGPT) assist in sub-domain discovery?

Answer

By generating and executing enumeration commands via prompts. Example prompts: "Discover all subdomains of google.com using dig" or "Use Sublist3r to gather subdomains of eccouncil." AI automates what would otherwise be manual command crafting.

→ TLDs and Sub-domains with AI Question

What does the Sublist3r command sublist3r -d eccouncil.org -o eccouncil_subdomains.txt do?

Answer

Enumerates sub-domains of eccouncil.org by searching multiple sources (Bing, Google, Netcraft, VirusTotal, etc.) and saves results to eccouncil_subdomains.txt.

→ Sublist3r Example Question

What is the Internet Archive Wayback Machine and why is it useful to attackers?

Answer

archive.org stores snapshots of websites since creation. Attackers can retrieve content removed from the target site — pages, images, audio/video, software — to craft phishing and web application attacks.

→ archive.org Question

What does the Photon flag --wayback do, and how does it differ from --only-urls?

Answer

--wayback fetches links from archive.org snapshots of the target.--only-urls retrieves archived URLs of the target without full snapshot crawling.

→ archive.org Question

Name four categories of data exposed by online people search services.

Answer

1. Personal identifiers (name, DOB, address, phone, email)2. Social and family connections (family members, social profiles)3. Professional details (profession, businesses, upcoming projects)4. Background data (property info, criminal records)

→ People Search Services Question

Name four people search services referenced in the CEH material.

Answer

Spokeo, Intelius, pipl, BeenVerified (also: Whitepages, Instant Checkmate, PeekYou).

→ People Search Services Question

What infrastructure details can attackers extract from job postings?

Answer

OS, software versions, firewall and server types, hypervisors, VMs, network appliances, database schema, and key employee email addresses.

→ Job Sites Question

Name four job sites attackers use for footprinting and what they target.

Answer

Dice, LinkedIn, Glassdoor, Simply Hired — used to extract infrastructure details from job postings and technical expertise/job history from employee resumes, identifying vulnerabilities in the target IT environment.

→ Job Sites Question

What is the difference between the surface web, deep web, and dark web?

Answer

Surface web: indexed, accessible via standard browsers.Deep web: unindexed, hidden — government/org databases; accessible via Tor or WWW Virtual Library.Dark web: subset of the deep web; fully anonymous; accessible only via specialized tools (Tor Browser, ExoneraTor).

→ Dark Web Footprinting Question

What is the role of Tor Browser in dark web footprinting?

Answer

Tor Browser acts as a default VPN, bouncing the user's IP through multiple servers. Attackers use it to access hidden content, unindexed sites, and encrypted dark web databases to gather confidential target data.

→ Tor Browser Question

Name five types of confidential data attackers gather from the dark web.

Answer

Credit card details · passport information · ID card details · medical records · social media accounts · Social Security Numbers (SSNs)

→ Dark Web Footprinting Question

What operator pattern is used to construct dark web search queries?

Answer

Combine: filetype: (target file type) + site:onion (restrict to .onion) + keyword — or use inurl: / intitle: to narrow by URL or page title.Example: filetype:sql site:onion dump finds database dumps; intitle:"login credentials" filetype:docx finds credential documents.

→ Dark Web Search Queries Question

What is OS fingerprinting and which three tools are used for it?

Answer

OS fingerprinting is the technique of detecting the operating system running at the target. Tools: Netcraft (site OS lookup), Shodan (connected devices and known CVEs), Censys (full internet-exposed asset inventory).

→ Determining the OS Question

What unique capability does Shodan offer beyond OS detection?

Answer

Shodan searches for known vulnerabilities and exploits across Exploit-DB, Metasploit, CVE, OSVDB, and Packetstorm in a single interface, alongside device discovery by city, country, hostname, and IP.

→ Determining the OS Question

What is competitive intelligence gathering and how does it differ from espionage?

Answer

CI gathering is the process of identifying, gathering, analyzing, verifying, and using competitor information from public sources. It is non-interfering, subtle, and legal — unlike industrial espionage or direct IP theft via hacking.

→ Competitive Intelligence Question

What is the difference between the direct and indirect approach in CI gathering?

Answer

Direct: primary source; trade shows, social engineering of employees/customers.Indirect: online resources; company websites, job ads, press releases, patents, financial filings, legal databases, search engines.

→ CI Approaches Question

What four questions does competitive intelligence help answer about a target company?

Answer

1. When did it begin? — history and establishment date2. How did it develop? — strategies, CRM, advertising3. Who leads it? — key decision-makers4. Where is it located? — branches and operations

→ What CI Helps Determine Question

What is EDGAR and what kind of information does it provide?

Answer

EDGAR (Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis, and Retrieval) is the SEC's system for automated collection and dissemination of mandatory corporate filings. It provides time-sensitive corporate information to improve transparency in the securities market.

→ CI Information Resources Question

Match these CI tools to their primary purpose: D&B Hoovers, LexisNexis, Factiva.

Answer

D&B Hoovers: 120M+ business records for sales intelligence and prospect targeting.LexisNexis: Legal, public records, and compliance data for risk/fraud/identity.Factiva: 33,000+ licensed sources — news, publications, newswires in 28 languages.

→ CI Information Resources Question

Which CI tool is used to research competitor patent and trademark registrations?

Answer

USPTO (uspto.gov) — the United States Patent and Trademark Office; provides patent/trademark registration data and search options for both databases.

→ CI Company Plans Question

Match these CI tools to their purpose: SEMRush, SimilarWeb, SERanking.

Answer

SEMRush: Competitor keyword research; Google keywords, AdWords, organic/paid rankings.SimilarWeb: Estimates website/app traffic, geography, and referral sources from aggregated data.SERanking: Traffic dynamics, keyword semantics, PPC competitor research.

→ CI Expert Opinions Question

What physical security information can attackers gather using geolocation tools, and which tools are used?

Answer

Building entrances, security cameras, gates, hiding spots, perimeter fence weak points, and utility connections. This enables planning of physical attacks (dumpster diving, surveillance, social engineering).Tools: Google Earth, Google Maps, Wikimapia.

→ Other Techniques Question

What information do financial services reveal, and which tools are used to gather it?

Answer

Market value of shares, company profile, competitor details, stock exchange rates, financial reports, press releases, and blog articles.Tools: Google Finance, MSN Money, Yahoo! Finance, Investing.com.

→ Other Techniques Question

What do business profile sites expose and which three are named in the CEH material?

Answer

Location, addresses, contact information, employee database, department names, and type of industry/service.Tools: opencorporates, Crunchbase, corporationwiki.

→ Other Techniques Question

What are alerting services and how do attackers use them for footprinting?

Answer

Content monitoring services that deliver automated notifications (email/SMS) when new content matches a defined search term. Attackers use them to passively track mentions of the target's name, members, website, and projects in real time.Tools: Google Alerts, X Alerts, Giga Alerts.

→ Other Techniques Question

What is Online Reputation Management (ORM) and how do attackers exploit it?

Answer

ORM monitors and improves a company's online reputation. The transparency it creates lets attackers collect genuine, up-to-date information — search rankings, mentions, social news, and online conversations about the target.Tools: Mention, ReviewPush, Reputology.

→ Other Techniques Question

What employee information can attackers gather from groups, forums, and blogs?

Answer

Full name, workplace/residence, phone numbers, personal and organizational email addresses, and photos (residence, workplace, awards). Attackers search by FQDNs, IP addresses, or usernames and may register with fake profiles in Google Groups or LinkedIn Groups.

→ Other Techniques Question

What sensitive data can be found in public source-code repositories, and what tool is used to discover them?

Answer

Configuration files, private SSH and SSL keys, source-code files, dynamic libraries, and software tools. Combined with active footprinting, this enables spear phishing and infrastructure attacks.Sites: GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, BitBucket.Tool: Recon-ng — a full-featured web reconnaissance framework.

→ Other Techniques Question

How is theHarvester used to gather information from LinkedIn, and what does each flag mean?

Answer

Command: theHarvester -d microsoft -l 200 -b linkedin-d = target domain/company name · -l = number of results · -b = data source (linkedin).Returns employee names and job titles for use in social engineering and targeted attacks.

→ Gathering Information from LinkedIn Question

What is the key difference between footprinting through social networking sites and footprinting through social engineering?

Answer

SNS footprinting: passively collects information users have already posted publicly — no deception, no interaction required.Social engineering footprinting: actively tricks people into revealing information through direct manipulation.

→ SNS vs. Social Engineering Footprinting Question

What search inputs can attackers use when searching for people on social networking sites, and what makes it anonymous?

Answer

Attackers search by name, email address, or physical address. Many platforms allow searching without registration, making people searches easy and anonymous. Some sites also reveal whether an account is active.

→ People Search on SNS Question

What categories of information can attackers collect from social networking sites like Facebook, LinkedIn, and Twitter?

Answer

Personal: name, position, organization, location, educational qualifications.Professional/contact: company, phone number, email, photos, videos.Behavioral (Twitter): advice, news, opinions, rumors, facts, announcements, and event details.

→ Types of Information Gathered Question

How do attackers harvest email lists from a target domain using theHarvester, and what is the purpose of the -f flag?

Answer

Command: theHarvester -d microsoft.com -l 200 -b baidu -f Microsoft_emails.xml-d = target domain · -l = result limit · -b = search engine source · -f = output file name (XML format).Harvested emails are used for social engineering and brute-force attacks.

→ Harvesting Email Lists Question

How can AI assist in email harvesting footprinting, and what is an example prompt?

Answer

AI tools like ChatGPT generate ready-to-run theHarvester commands from natural-language prompts. Example: "Use theHarvester to gather email accounts associated with 'microsoft.com', limiting results to 200, and leveraging 'baidu' as a data source." AI automates command crafting, lowering the attacker's skill requirement.

→ Harvesting Email Lists with AI Question

What is BuzzSumo and how do attackers use it during social media footprinting?

Answer

BuzzSumo is an advanced social search engine that finds the most shared content for a topic, author, or domain across Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, Pinterest, and Google Plus. Attackers use it to track shared content related to a target domain and collect social media accounts, URLs, and email addresses for phishing and social engineering.

→ Analyzing Target Social Media Presence Question

Name four tools used to analyze a target's social media presence and what each does.

Answer

BuzzSumo: most shared content by domain/topic/author.Google Trends: search term popularity over time.Hashatit: real-time hashtag tracking across social networks.Ubersuggest: keyword and top content research for a target domain.

→ Analyzing Target Social Media Presence Question

What does the Sherlock tool do and what does its output reveal?

Answer

Sherlock searches a large number of social networking sites for a target username and returns the full profile URL on every site where that username exists — enabling rapid cross-platform profiling of an individual.Command: sherlock 'Elon Musk'

→ SNS Footprinting Tools Question

What is Social Searcher and what attacker-relevant data does it expose?

Answer

Social Searcher performs real-time content searches across social networks and provides deep analytics. Attackers use it to track a target's profile URLs, postings, and personal information across platforms.

→ SNS Footprinting Tools Question

How can AI assist in SNS footprinting with Sherlock, and what does the --output flag do?

Answer

AI (e.g., ChatGPT) generates Sherlock commands from natural-language prompts. Example prompt: "Use Sherlock to gather personal information about Sundar Pichai and save the result in recon2.txt."Command: sherlock SundarPichai --output recon2--output recon2 saves all discovered profile URLs to a file named recon2.

→ SNS Footprinting with AI Question

What is Whois and on which port does it operate?

Answer

Whois is a query and response protocol for querying databases that store registered users or assignees of an Internet resource (domain name, IP address block, or autonomous system). It listens on port 43 (TCP).

→ Whois Lookup Question

What are the three Whois data models?

Answer

Thick Whois (Distributed): stores complete Whois info from all registrars.Thin Whois (Centralized): stores only the registrar's Whois server name; full details held by that server.Decentralized Whois: stores complete info with multiple independent entities managing the database.

→ Whois Data Models Question

Name five pieces of information a Whois query returns.

Answer

Domain name details · domain registrar · contact details of the domain owner · domain name servers · NetRange · creation date · expiry records · last updated record · domain status · IP address information

→ What a Whois Query Returns Question

How do attackers use information obtained from a Whois lookup?

Answer

1. Create a map of the organization's network2. Mislead domain owners with social engineering3. Obtain internal details of the network

→ How Attackers Use Whois Data Question

Name the five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) and their regions.

Answer

ARIN – North America · AFRINIC – Africa · APNIC – Asia-Pacific · RIPE NCC – Europe/Middle East · LACNIC – Latin America & Caribbean

→ Regional Internet Registries Question

What makes Batch IP Converter useful for Whois footprinting?

Answer

It provides country, state/province, city, phone, fax, network provider, administrator, and technical-support contact info for an IP address, hostname, or domain. It supports Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and IPv6.

→ Whois Lookup Tools Question

What types of information does IP geolocation provide about a target?

Answer

Country, region/state, city, latitude/longitude, ZIP/postal code, time zone, connection speed, ISP (hosting company), domain name, IDD country code, area code, weather station code and name, mobile carrier, and elevation.

→ Finding IP Geolocation Information Question

How do attackers leverage IP geolocation data, and which tools provide it?

Answer

Attackers use it to launch social engineering attacks (spamming, phishing), perform surveillance and non-technical attacks (dumpster diving, hoaxing), set up compromised servers near the victim, or deploy location-specific malware.Tools: IP2Location, IP Location Finder, IP Address Geographical Location Finder.

→ IP Geolocation Lookup Tools Question

What is DNS footprinting and where does it fall in the footprinting methodology?

Answer

DNS footprinting is the phase immediately following Whois footprinting. Attackers query DNS infrastructure to collect information about DNS servers, DNS records, and server types used by the target organization.

→ DNS Footprinting Question

What attacker value does DNS footprinting provide?

Answer

It allows attackers to identify hosts connected to the target network, forming the basis for further exploitation of the target organization.

→ DNS Footprinting – Purpose Question

What are the three key techniques used in DNS footprinting?

Answer

DNS record extraction: querying for various record types to enumerate infrastructure.Reverse DNS lookups: resolving IPs back to hostnames to map the network.DNS interrogation tools: automated tools that systematically query DNS servers at scale.

→ DNS Footprinting – Key Techniques Question

What does DNS zone data contain, and how do attackers use it?

Answer

DNS zone data includes DNS domain names, computer names, IP addresses, and more. Attackers use it to determine key hosts in the network and then perform social engineering attacks to gather even more information.

→ Extracting DNS Information Question

What DNS record type maps an IP address to a hostname, and which maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?

Answer

PTR maps an IP address to a hostname (reverse lookup).AAAA maps a hostname to an IPv6 address.

→ DNS Record Types Question

What DNS record types should you know for the exam? (List all 11)

Answer

A – host IP | AAAA – host IPv6 | MX – mail server | NS – name server | CNAME – alias | SOA – domain authority | SRV – service records | PTR – IP→hostname | RP – responsible person | HINFO – CPU & OS info | TXT – unstructured text

→ DNS Record Types Question

Name five DNS interrogation tools and the condition that makes DNS zone transfer easy for an attacker.

Answer

Tools: SecurityTrails, Fierce, DNSChecker, zdns, DNSdumpster.com.Condition: if the target network allows unknown, unauthorized users to transfer DNS zone data, an attacker can easily obtain DNS information using these tools.

→ DNS Interrogation Tools Question

What does SecurityTrails do and what record types does it enumerate?

Answer

SecurityTrails is an advanced DNS enumeration tool that creates a DNS map of the target domain network. It enumerates current and historical DNS records (A, AAAA, NS, MX, SOA, TXT) and all existing subdomains using brute-force techniques.

→ SecurityTrails Question

What does the Fierce --traverse 10 option do?

Answer

It instructs Fierce to search for contiguous blocks of IPs within a range of 10, scanning domains near the discovered records of the target.

→ Fierce Question

How can attackers use AI to perform DNS enumeration, and what tool does it invoke?

Answer

Attackers can prompt ChatGPT or other generative AI to automate DNS lookup tasks. For example, prompting it to "Install and use DNSRecon to perform DNS enumeration on the target domain" generates a shell command using dnsrecon with standard enumeration techniques (-t std).

→ DNS Lookup with AI Question

What is the difference between a DNS lookup and a reverse DNS lookup?

Answer

DNS lookup: converts a domain name into an IP address.Reverse DNS lookup: obtains the domain name of a given IP address by locating a DNS PTR record.

→ Reverse DNS Lookup Question

What does the DNSRecon -r option do, and what is an example command?

Answer

The -r option specifies the range of IP addresses (first to last) for a reverse lookup by brute force.Example: dnsrecon -r 162.241.216.0-162.241.216.255

→ DNSRecon Question

Name five tools used for reverse DNS lookup.

Answer

DNSRecon, Reverse Lookup (mxtoolbox.com), puredns, Reverse IP Domain Check, and Reverse IP Lookup.

→ Reverse DNS Lookup Question

How does an attacker find the network range of a target using ARIN?

Answer

Enter the target's server IP address (gathered during Whois footprinting) into the ARIN Whois database search tool. The result yields the full network range of the target.

→ ARIN Whois Database Question

What four types of information does the network range reveal to an attacker?

Answer

1. Network structure — how the network is organized and which machines are alive2. Network topology — layout of the target network3. Access control devices — firewalls, routers, gateways4. Operating systems — OS types in use

→ What Network Range Reveals Question

What are the three IANA-reserved private IP address ranges?

Answer

10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255 (10/8 prefix)172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 (172.16/12 prefix)192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255 (192.168/16 prefix)

→ IANA Private IP Ranges Question

Name two widely used traceroute tools in network footprinting.

Answer

NetScanTools Pro and PingPlotter.

→ Traceroute and DNS Misconfiguration Question

How can improperly configured DNS servers and traceroute aid an attacker during network footprinting?

Answer

Misconfigured DNS servers may expose a list of internal machines in the network. Traceroute can reveal the internal IP address of the gateway, providing further internal network details.

→ DNS Misconfiguration Question

What protocol and IP header field does traceroute use, and what four types of information does it reveal?

Answer

Uses ICMP protocol and the TTL field. Reveals: number of hops, round-trip time (RTT) between routers, router names and network affiliation, and geographic locations of intermediate hops.

→ Traceroute Question

How does the TTL mechanism work in traceroute?

Answer

Each router decrements TTL by 1. When TTL=0, the router discards the packet and returns an ICMP error message to the source. Traceroute starts with TTL=1 and increments by 1 per probe, recording each hop until the destination responds with an ICMP reply.

→ How TTL Works Question

What are the three traceroute types, their protocols, and their commands?

Answer

ICMP (Windows default): tracert <target>TCP (Layer 4, Linux): sudo tcptraceroute <target>UDP (Linux default): traceroute <target>TCP/UDP are used when ICMP is blocked by network devices.

→ Traceroute Types Question

How can AI assist an attacker in performing tracerouting?

Answer

An attacker prompts an AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT) with a natural-language request such as "Perform network tracerouting to discover the routers on the path to a target host." The AI generates and executes the appropriate command: traceroute <target>.

→ Traceroute with AI Question

What does traceroute analysis across multiple runs reveal about a target network?

Answer

By comparing last few hops across multiple traceroutes to different hosts, an attacker identifies intermediate routers and firewalls and reconstructs the network topology — including device positions and DMZ structure.

→ Traceroute Analysis Question

What distinguishes NetScanTools Pro from PingPlotter?

Answer

NetScanTools Pro: Supports ICMP, UDP, or TCP traceroute; identifies intermediate devices; maps country per IPv4 hop.PingPlotter: Tracks latency and packet loss over time; visualizes data in graphs; identifies bandwidth bottlenecks, WiFi interference, and hardware faults.

→ Traceroute Tools Question

What is email tracking and what do attackers use it for?

Answer

Email tracking monitors delivery and opening of emails via digitally time-stamped records. Attackers use it to collect IP addresses, mail servers, and service provider details to build a hacking strategy and perform social engineering.

→ Tracking Email Communications Question

Name five types of information gathered from a target via email tracking tools.

Answer

Recipient's IP address · Geolocation · Whether email was read (and read duration) · OS and browser version · Device type (desktop/mobile/laptop) · Path travelled through email transfer agents · Whether links were clicked · Whether the email was forwarded

→ Information Gathered via Email Tracking Question

What seven fields does an email header expose to an attacker?

Answer

1. Sender's mail server2. Date/time received by originator's email servers3. Authentication system used by sender's mail server4. Date/time message was sent5. Unique message ID6. Sender's full name7. Sender's IP address and sending address

→ Email Header Question

What distinguishes eMailTrackerPro from IP2LOCATION's Email Header Tracer?

Answer

eMailTrackerPro: Analyzes email headers to extract geographical location and IP; saves past traces for later review.IP2LOCATION Email Header Tracer: Open-source service; traces email path and mail servers using IP addresses in the header.

→ Email Tracking Tools Question

What is social engineering in the context of footprinting?

Answer

A non-technical process in which an attacker misleads a person into providing confidential information inadvertently. The target is unaware that someone is stealing confidential data. Attackers exploit the gullible nature of people and their willingness to share information.

→ Social Engineering Overview Question

What is the two-step process an attacker follows when performing social engineering footprinting?

Answer

1. Gain the confidence of an authorized user.2. Mislead that user into revealing confidential information.

→ Social Engineering Overview Question

What categories of information do social engineers attempt to gather during footprinting?

Answer

Credit card details and social security numbers · usernames and passwords · security products in use · OS and software versions · IP addresses and names of servers · network layout information · other personal information

→ Information Gathered Question

Name the social engineering techniques used in footprinting.

Answer

Eavesdropping · shoulder surfing · dumpster diving · impersonation · tailgating · piggybacking · third-party authorization · reverse social engineering

→ Techniques Question

What malicious purposes does an attacker pursue using information obtained through social engineering?

Answer

Gaining unauthorized access to systems · identity theft · industrial espionage · network intrusion · fraud

→ Goals and Malicious Uses Question

How do attackers use social networking sites to gather information through social engineering?

Answer

By browsing public profiles (no barrier to access) or by creating fake profiles to pose as genuine users and lure victims. If a victim accepts a friend request from a fake account, the attacker gains access to restricted pages as well.

→ Collecting Information via SNS Question

What does an attacker learn when a user shares photos and videos on a social networking site?

Answer

Identity of family members, interests, and related information — especially when the user has not set appropriate privacy settings for their albums.

→ What Attackers Get from User Activity Question

What attacker-relevant information does an organization's recruitment activity on social networking sites reveal?

Answer

Platform/technology information — job postings and recruitment content often disclose the technologies and platforms the organization uses.

→ What Attackers Get from Organizational Activity Question

What five types of information can an attacker obtain by monitoring organizational activity on social networking sites?

Answer

Business strategies (user surveys) · product profile (product promotion) · social engineering opportunities (user support) · platform/technology information (recruitment) · type of business (background checks to hire employees)

→ What Attackers Get from Organizational Activity Question

What is eavesdropping and what forms of communication can it target?

Answer

The unauthorized interception of communication — in any form: audio, video, or text — without the consent of the communicating parties. Includes tapping phone conversations and reading messages from instant messaging or fax transmissions.

→ Eavesdropping Question

What is shoulder surfing and what types of data does it target?

Answer

Secretly observing the target to capture critical information. The attacker stands behind the victim and watches keystrokes or screen activity. Effective for capturing passwords, PINs, security codes, account numbers, and credit card information. Easiest to perform in crowded places.

→ Shoulder Surfing Question

What is dumpster diving (trashing) and what sources does an attacker target?

Answer

Rummaging through garbage to find sensitive information. Sources: trash bins, printer waste bins, sticky notes at desks, and ATM trash bins. Yields phone bills, contact info, financial info, operations-related info, and printouts of source code or sensitive data.

→ Dumpster Diving Question

What is impersonation as a social engineering technique, and what roles might an attacker assume?

Answer

Pretending to be a legitimate or authorized person — courier, janitor, technician, client, or visitor — and using phones or other media to mislead targets. The attacker then scans terminals for passwords, searches documents on desks, rummages bins, or shoulder surfs.

→ Impersonation Question

What is Maltego used for in footprinting?

Answer

Determining relationships and real-world links between people, groups, organizations, websites, Internet infrastructure, and documents. Attackers add a Website entity with the target's domain to extract email addresses, phone numbers, DNS names, Netblocks, and IP addresses.

→ Maltego Question

What is Recon-ng and which module do attackers use to enumerate target hosts?

Answer

A web reconnaissance framework with independent modules for open-source, web-based reconnaissance. Attackers use the recon/domains-hosts/brute_hosts module to extract a list of hosts associated with a target URL.

→ Recon-ng Question

What does FOCA stand for and what is its primary purpose?

Answer

Fingerprinting Organizations with Collected Archives — a tool used mainly to find metadata and hidden information in scanned documents (Microsoft Office, Open Office, PDF). Also performs web search, DNS search, IP resolution, PTR scanning, and dictionary attacks against DNS.

→ FOCA Question

What are the four OSINT Framework tool indicators and what does each mean?

Answer

(T) – must be installed and run locally · (D) – Google Dork · (R) – requires registration · (M) – URL containing the search term that must be edited manually

→ OSINT Framework Question

What distinguishes subfinder from FOCA as footprinting tools?

Answer

subfinder is a passive subdomain discovery tool that finds valid subdomains using online sources (supports JSON, file, stdout output).FOCA finds metadata and hidden information inside scanned documents and performs DNS/IP resolution and PTR scanning.

→ subfinder Question

Name the six AI use cases in OSINT and what each does.

Answer

Web Scraping – automates data extraction from social media, blogs, deep web · Pattern Recognition – ML identifies entities and relationships · Content Summarization – NLP extracts key info from large datasets · Sentiment Analysis – interprets emotions from text · Image Recognition – face ID, metadata, deepfake detection · AI Detection – identifies AI-generated content

→ AI Use Cases in OSINT Question

What are the four benefits of integrating AI in OSINT?

Answer

Improved Efficiency – automates scraping and extraction · Greater Scope – covers surface, deep, and dark web · Enhanced Visibility – connects data points into graphical networks · Increased Investigator Safety – enables anonymized, automated investigations

→ Benefits of AI in OSINT Question

What is Taranis AI and what are its four key features?

Answer

An advanced OSINT tool using NLP and AI to collect unstructured news articles and transform them into reports and PDFs.Features: Advanced OSINT Capabilities · AI-Enhanced Analysis · Multi-Format Output · Seamless Publishing

→ Taranis AI Question

What is OSS Insight and what dataset does it analyze?

Answer

An AI-powered tool that analyzes over five billion GitHub events to provide insights into repositories, developer productivity, and collaboration patterns. Its GPT-Powered Data Explorer lets users query GitHub data using natural language.

→ OSS Insight Question

What is DorkGPT and how does it differ from DorkGenius?

Answer

Both are AI-powered Google Dorking tools.DorkGPT uses GPT models to generate and refine advanced search queries for finding sensitive information and hidden pages.DorkGenius automates Google Dorking to uncover hidden files, directories, and security vulnerabilities.

→ Additional AI-Powered OSINT Tools Question

What four functions does an AI-generated Python footprinting script typically define, and what tool does each use?

Answer

dns_lookup – dig · whois_lookup – whois · email_enumeration – theHarvester · run_footprinting – orchestrates and prints results of all three

→ Custom Python Scripts with AI Question

What are footprinting countermeasures?

Answer

Measures or actions taken to prevent or offset information disclosure to potential attackers. They span web infrastructure, published content, personnel behavior, network protocols, and physical location.

→ Footprinting Countermeasures Question

Name four web and DNS hardening countermeasures against footprinting.

Answer

1. Configure web servers and IIS to avoid information leakage and banner grabbing.2. Disable directory listings in web servers.3. Use split DNS and restrict zone transfer to authorized servers only.4. Avoid domain-level cross-linking for critical assets.

→ Web and DNS Hardening Question

What publication and information control countermeasures prevent footprinting?

Answer

Limit website content; avoid disclosing critical info in press releases and annual reports; prevent search engine caching; use anonymous registration services; request archive.org to remove site history; keep the domain name profile private; place critical documents offline; do not display sensitive plans on notice boards.

→ Information and Publication Control Question

What two network-level countermeasures hide an organization's IP address from footprinters?

Answer

1. Implement a VPN to mask the real IP address.2. Keep the server behind a secure proxy.

→ Network and Protocol Defense Question

What countermeasure prevents automated footprinting tools from rapidly collecting information from public-facing services?

Answer

Implement captchas and rate limiting on public-facing services to slow or block automated collection tools.

→ Network and Protocol Defense Question

Name four personnel and awareness countermeasures against footprinting.

Answer

1. Restrict employee access to social networking sites from the organization's network.2. Educate employees to use pseudonyms on blogs, groups, and forums.3. Conduct periodic security awareness training about social engineering tricks.4. Train employees to thwart social engineering attacks.

→ Personnel and Awareness Question

Name three geolocation-specific countermeasures against footprinting.

Answer

1. Disable geo-tagging functionality on cameras to prevent geolocation tracking.2. Avoid revealing location or travel plans on social networking sites.3. Turn off geolocation access on all mobile devices when not required.

→ Physical and Location Security Question

How do honeypots and honeynets serve as a footprinting countermeasure?

Answer

Deployed within the network, they attract and detect attackers while diverting potential footprinters away from critical systems — functioning as both a detection mechanism and a deception tool.

→ Detection and Deception

docs.title: Footprinting Concepts
docs.text: Footprinting acts as a preparatory phase for the attacker, who needs to gather as much information as possible to find ways to intrude into the target network. This section covers what footprinting is, why it is necessary, and its objectives.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Reconnaissance (also known as footprinting) is the preparatory phase where an attacker seeks to gather as much information as possible about a target of evaluation prior to launching an attack.

Footprinting is the first step in ethical hacking. It involves collecting information about a target network and its environment to uncover vulnerabilities and identify exploitation paths. The result is a blueprint — a unique system profile of the target organization.

Key characteristics:

  • No single methodology; information can be traced in multiple ways
  • Must be carried out in an organized, methodical manner
  • Identifies the level of risk associated with publicly accessible information
  • Uncovers vulnerabilities and ways to exploit them before the attack phase

docs.title: Types of Footprinting
docs.text:
Exam-critical 🎯

Passive Active Interaction No direct interaction with the target Direct interaction with the target Detectability Difficult to detect Target may recognize the activity Preparation Less preparation needed More preparation required; may leave traces Examples OSINT, search engines, social networking sites DNS interrogation, social engineering, port scanning

docs.title: Passive Footprinting
docs.text:
Gathering information without direct interaction. Useful when the activity must not be detected. Only archived and stored information is collected.

It involves:

  • Open-source Intelligence (OSINT) gathering
  • Proprietary databases and paid services
  • Sharing intelligence with partner organizations or industry groups

docs.title: Active Footprinting
docs.text:
Gathering information with direct interaction. The target may recognize the ongoing process. Requires more preparation as it may leave traces.

It involves:

  • DNS interrogation
  • Social engineering
  • Network/port scanning
  • User and service enumeration

docs.title: Information Obtained in Footprinting
docs.text:
The major objectives of footprinting include collecting network, system, and organizational information about the target. Such information helps attackers gain access to sensitive data or perform various attacks.

Organization Information Network Information System Information Employee details (names, contact, designation) Domain and sub-domains Web server OS Addresses and phone numbers Network blocks Location of web servers Branch and location details Network topology, trusted routers, and firewalls Publicly available email addresses Background of the organization IP addresses of reachable systems Usernames and passwords Web technologies Whois records News articles, press releases, related documents DNS records Legal documents, patents, trademarks

docs.title: Objectives of Footprinting
docs.text:
• Build a hacking strategy by mapping the target organization's network
  • Identify the easiest way to breach the security perimeter
  • Obtain an outline of the security posture: placement of firewalls, proxies, and other solutions
  • Reduce an unknown entity to a specific range of domain names, network blocks, and IP addresses
  • Identify vulnerabilities in target systems to select appropriate exploits
  • Build an information database of security weaknesses to find the weakest link

docs.title: Footprinting Threats
docs.text: Threat Description Social Engineering Hackers collect information through persuasion; willing employees unknowingly reveal sensitive data System and Network Attacks Information about OS and configuration is used to find and exploit vulnerabilities, potentially taking control of systems or the entire network Information Leakage Sensitive data in attacker hands enables targeted attacks or monetary exploitation Privacy Loss Attackers access systems and escalate privileges to admin level, compromising privacy of the organization and its personnel Corporate Espionage Competitors use footprinting to acquire sensitive data, launch similar products, alter prices, and undermine market position Business Loss Malicious attacks enabled by footprinting cost organizations — especially e-commerce, banking, and finance — billions annually

docs.title: Footprinting Methodology
docs.text:
The footprinting methodology is a procedure for collecting information about a target organization from all available sources — URLs, locations, establishment details, employee count, domain ranges, contact information, and more. Attackers collect this information from publicly accessible sources such as search engines, social networking sites, and Whois databases.

They address every layer at which footprinting can expose organizational data — web infrastructure, published content, personnel behavior, network protocols, and physical location.

  • Configure IIS to avoid information disclosure through banner grabbing.
  • Disable directory listings in web servers.
  • Set apart internal and external DNS or use split DNS; restrict zone transfer to authorized servers only.
  • Do not enable protocols that are not required.
  • Always use TCP/IP and IPsec filters for defense in depth.
  • Avoid domain-level cross-linking for critical assets.

docs.title: Information and Publication Control
docs.text:
• Limit the amount of information published on a website or the Internet.
  • Do not reveal critical information in press releases, annual reports, product catalogues, etc.
  • Prevent search engines from caching a web page; use anonymous registration services.
  • Request archive.org to delete the history of the website from the archive database.
  • Keep the domain name profile private.
  • Place critical documents (business plans, proprietary documents) offline to prevent exploitation.
  • Ensure no critical information (strategic plans, product information, sales projections) is displayed on notice boards or walls.

docs.title: Access, Identity, and Privacy
docs.text:
• Develop and enforce security policies (information security and password policies) to regulate what employees can reveal to third parties.
  • Implement multi-factor authentication to enhance security of systems and resources.
  • Encrypt and password-protect sensitive information.
  • Opt for privacy services on a Whois lookup database.
  • Sanitize details provided to Internet registrars to hide the organization's direct contact details.
  • Disable or delete accounts of employees who have left the organization.

docs.title: Network and Protocol Defense
docs.text:
• Hide the IP address and related information by implementing a VPN or keeping the server behind a secure proxy.
  • Implement captchas and rate limiting on public-facing services to prevent automated information collection.
  • Configure mail servers to ignore mails from anonymous individuals.

docs.title: Personnel and Awareness
docs.text:
• Restrict employee access to social networking sites from the organization's network.
  • Educate employees to use pseudonyms on blogs, groups, and forums.
  • Conduct security awareness training periodically about social engineering tricks and risks.
  • Train employees to thwart social engineering techniques and attacks.

docs.title: Physical and Location Security
docs.text:
• Disable the geo-tagging functionality on cameras to prevent geolocation tracking.
  • Avoid revealing one's location or travel plans on social networking sites.
  • Turn off geolocation access on all mobile devices when not required.

docs.title: Detection and Deception
docs.text:
• Use footprinting techniques to discover and remove any sensitive information that is publicly available.
  • Deploy honeypots or honeynets within the network to attract and detect attackers, diverting potential footprinters away from critical systems.

docs.title: Custom Python Scripts with AI
docs.text:
Attackers can use AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT to create and run custom footprinting scripts. By providing an appropriate prompt, the AI generates a ready-to-run script that executes a series of footprinting commands against a target domain.

Example prompt:

"Develop a Python script which will accept the domain name www.microsoft.com as input and execute a series of website footprinting commands, including DNS lookups, WHOIS records retrieval, email enumeration, and more, to gather information about the target domain."

The generated script defines four functions:

Full script – website_footprinting.py 
import subprocess

def dns_lookup(domain):
    return subprocess.getoutput(f"dig {domain} ANY +noall +answer")

def whois_lookup(domain):
    return subprocess.getoutput(f"whois {domain}")

def email_enumeration(domain):
    return subprocess.getoutput(f"theHarvester -d {domain} -b all -l 100")

def run_footprinting(domain):
    print("Performing DNS Lookup...")
    print(dns_lookup(domain))
    print("\nPerforming Whois Lookup...")
    print(whois_lookup(domain))
    print("\nEnumerating Emails...")
    print(email_enumeration(domain))

domain = 'www.microsoft.com'
run_footprinting(domain)
Function Tool Used Purpose dns_lookup(domain) dig Performs a DNS lookup for the specified domain whois_lookup(domain) whois Retrieves WHOIS records for the specified domain email_enumeration(domain) theHarvester Enumerates email addresses associated with the domain run_footprinting(domain) — Orchestrates and prints results of all three functions

The script is run with python3 website_footprinting.py to perform automated footprinting on the target domain.

docs.title: Footprinting through Internet Research Services
docs.text:
Internet research services — including people search, alerting, financial services, and job sites — expose sensitive target information such as infrastructure details, physical location, and employee data. Attackers use this to build targeted hacking strategies against an organization's network.

Key activities covered here: discovering top-level domains and sub-domains, geolocation, people search services, job site intelligence, financial services, third-party data repositories, dark web footprinting, and competitive intelligence gathering.

docs.title: Finding a Company's Top-Level Domains (TLDs) and Sub-domains
docs.text:
A company's TLDs represent its public-facing web presence — designed for customers and partners, and locatable via search engines such as Google and Bing. They may expose organizational history, services, products, and contact information.

Sub-domains are typically restricted to employees or specific departments. Administrators often create sub-domains for testing before production deployment; these are frequently insecure and more vulnerable to exploitation. Sub-domains can reveal:

  • Departmental structure and business units
  • Source code or documents hosted on webservers
  • Private organizational functions
  • Access controls based on IP, domain, subnet, or credentials

Because most organizations use predictable sub-domain formats, an attacker who knows the external URL can discover sub-domains by trial and error or by using dedicated tools.

Google Advanced Search Operator:

site:microsoft.com -inurl:www

docs.title: Tools for Sub-domain Discovery

docs.title: Finding TLDs and Sub-domains with AI
docs.text: Attackers can use AI-powered tools (e.g., ChatGPT) to generate and execute sub-domain enumeration commands, automating what would otherwise be a manual process.

docs.title: Example 1 — dig via ChatGPT prompt
docs.text:
Prompt: "Discover all the subdomains of 'google.com' using dig command."

dig +short google.com NS | xargs -I{} dig +nocmd +noall +answer @{} google.com | grep -E 'CNAME|A|AAAA'
Command part Purpose dig +short google.com NS Retrieves NS records for the domain in shortened format | xargs -I{} Passes each name server as an argument to the next command dig +nocmd +noall +answer @{} google.com Queries each NS for A records, returning IP addresses of sub-domains

docs.title: Example 2 — Sublist3r via ChatGPT prompt
docs.text:
Prompt: "Use Sublist3r to gather a list of subdomains of the target organization eccouncil."

sublist3r -d eccouncil.org -o eccouncil_subdomains.txt
Flag Meaning -d eccouncil.org Target domain to enumerate -o eccouncil_subdomains.txt Output file for the results

Sublist3r searches multiple sources (Bing, Google, Netcraft, VirusTotal, etc.) and saves discovered sub-domains to the specified file.

docs.title: Extracting Website Information from archive.org
docs.text:
The Internet Archive Wayback Machine (archive.org) stores snapshots of websites since their creation, allowing an attacker to retrieve content that has since been removed — including web pages, images, audio/video files, and software programs. This historical data can be used to craft phishing attacks or other web application attacks against the target.

Photon is a tool that automates retrieval of archived content from archive.org.

Command Purpose photon.py -u <URL> -l 3 -t 200 --wayback Retrieve archive.org links of the target website python photon.py -u <URL> -l 3 -t 200 --only-urls Retrieve archived URLs of the target website Flag Meaning -u <URL> Target website URL -l 3 Crawl depth level -t 200 Number of threads --wayback Fetch links from archive.org snapshots --only-urls Output URLs only

docs.title: Footprinting through People Search Services
docs.text:
Online people search services (e.g., Spokeo, Intelius, pipl, BeenVerified, Whitepages, Instant Checkmate, PeekYou) aggregate public records and can expose:

  • Names, addresses, phone numbers, date of birth, photographs, videos
  • Profession, businesses owned, upcoming projects, operating environment
  • Websites and blogs, social networking profiles, property information
  • Company email addresses, cell/fax numbers, personal email addresses
  • Optional background and criminal check data

Attackers use this data to attempt to obtain bank details, credit card information, and personal history — enabling targeted social engineering and other attacks.

Spokeo (spokeo.com) is a commonly cited example: it returns phone numbers, email addresses, address history, age, family members, social profiles, and court records for individuals associated with a target organization.

docs.title: Footprinting through Job Sites
docs.text:
Job postings and employee resumes on sites such as Dice, LinkedIn, Glassdoor, and Simply Hired inadvertently disclose infrastructure details. Attackers extract:

Source Information revealed Job postings OS, software versions, firewall/server types, hypervisors, VMs, network appliances, database schema Employee resumes Technical expertise, educational qualifications, job history, technologies used Key employee lists Email addresses and roles

This information helps attackers identify underlying vulnerabilities in the target IT infrastructure and tailor attacks accordingly.

The dark web enables anonymous navigation and is used by attackers to gather confidential target data: credit card details, passport and ID information, medical records, social media accounts, Social Security Numbers (SSNs).

docs.text:

Search engines can expose technology platforms, employee details, login pages, intranet portals, and contact information — enabling social engineering and advanced system attacks.

docs.title: Footprinting Using Advanced Google Hacking Techniques
docs.text:
A simple search (e.g., "Microsoft") can reveal physical location, contact addresses, services, and employee count. Major search engines include Google, Bing, Yahoo, Baidu, Yandex, DuckDuckGo, and WolframAlpha.

Google hacking is the use of advanced Google search operators to build complex queries that extract sensitive or hidden information and identify vulnerable targets. Attackers also use the Google Hacking Database (GHDB) — a curated collection of queries for finding sensitive data.

docs.text:
Attackers can leverage AI-powered technologies to enhance and automate footprinting tasks. Tools such as ShellGPT allow attackers to generate precise shell commands from natural-language prompts.

Example prompt:

"Use filetype search operator to obtain pdf files on the target website eccouncil.org and store the result in the recon1.txt file"

docs.title: Generated Shell Command
docs.text:
lynx --dump "http://www.google.com/search?q=site:eccouncil.org+filetype:pdf" \
  | grep "http" \
  | cut -d "=" -f2 \
  | grep -o "http[^&]*" > recon1.txt

docs.title: Command Breakdown
docs.text: Segment Purpose lynx --dump "..." Opens Google search results for PDFs on eccouncil.org in text/dump mode \| grep "http" Keeps only lines containing URLs \| cut -d "=" -f2 Splits on = and takes the second field (the URL value) \| grep -o "http[^&]*" Extracts the clean URL, stopping before any & parameter > recon1.txt Saves all results to recon1.txt

docs.title: Google Hacking Database (GHDB)
docs.text:
Source: exploit-db.com/google-hacking-database

The GHDB is a subset of the Exploit-DB focused on Google Dorks — advanced search queries that uncover sensitive information inadvertently exposed on the web.

docs.title: What GHDB Queries Uncover
docs.text:
• Sensitive files — configuration files, database dumps, log files with credentials
  • Exposed directories — open directories on web servers
  • Error messages — revealing server configurations or vulnerabilities
  • Vulnerable devices — specific device types or software versions with known vulnerabilities

docs.title: GHDB Categories
docs.text: Category Description Footholds Queries that help establish an initial access point into a target system or network Files Containing Usernames Pages or files that expose usernames, often found in config or log files Sensitive Directories Open or misconfigured directories on web servers exposing internal content Web Server Detection Queries that identify the type and version of a web server Vulnerable Files Files associated with known vulnerabilities, such as unpatched scripts or outdated components Vulnerable Servers Servers running software versions with known exploitable weaknesses Error Messages Server or application error pages that reveal configurations or stack traces Files Containing Juicy Info Files with miscellaneous sensitive data not covered by more specific categories Files Containing Passwords Files that directly expose passwords or hashed credentials Sensitive Online Shopping Info Exposed e-commerce data such as order details, customer records, or payment info Network or Vulnerability Data IDS/firewall logs, network maps, or vulnerability scan results left publicly accessible Pages Containing Login Portals Login pages for admin panels, VPNs, webmail, and other authenticated services Various Online Devices Publicly accessible IoT devices, cameras, routers, and industrial control panels Advisories and Vulnerabilities Pages referencing specific CVEs, security advisories, or known exploit details

docs.title: How Attackers Leverage the GHDB
docs.text:
• Reconnaissance — gather info on exposed files, directories, and devices
  • Exploiting Misconfigurations — gain unauthorized access via misconfigured servers
  • Finding Vulnerable Systems — locate outdated or unpatched software versions
  • Credential Harvesting — extract usernames and passwords for stuffing or brute force
  • Identifying Open Ports and Services — map potential entry points on a network

docs.title: SearchSploit
docs.text: SearchSploit is a command-line search tool for Exploit-DB that allows offline searching through a locally checked-out copy of the repository. Useful for assessments on air-gapped or segregated networks without Internet access.

docs.title: VPN Footprinting through Google Hacking Database
docs.text: Google dorks can be used to footprint Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), revealing login portals, key directories, and VPN server details.

docs.title: Google Dorks for VPN Footprinting
docs.text: Google Dork Purpose inurl:"/sslvpn_logon.shtml" intitle:"User Authentication" "WatchGuard Technologies" Finds pages containing login portals inurl:/sslvpn/Login/Login Finds VPN login portals site:vpn.*.*/ intitle:"login" Finds VPN login portals inurl:weblogin + intitle:("USG20-VPN"\|"USG20W-VPN"\|USG40\|…\|"FLEX") Finds hosts with Zyxel hardcoded password vulnerability intext:Please Login SSL VPN inurl:remote/login + intext:FortiClient Finds Fortinet VPN login pages site:vpn.*.*/ intext:"login" intitle:"login" Retrieves various VPN login pages intitle:"index of" /etc/openvpn/ Retrieves juicy info and sensitive directories "-----BEGIN OpenVPN Static key V1-----" ext:key Finds OpenVPN static keys intitle:"index of" "vpn-config.*" Retrieves juicy info about vpn-config files Index of / *.ovpn Finds OpenVPN config files, certificates, and keys inurl:"/vpn/tmindex.html" vpn Finds Netscaler and Citrix Gateway VPN login portals intitle:"SSL VPN Service" + intext:"Your system administrator provided the following information…" Finds Cisco ASA login web pages

docs.title: VPN Footprinting through GHDB with AI
docs.text:
Attackers can use AI tools such as ChatGPT to generate dork-based shell commands for VPN footprinting.

Example prompt:

"Use inurl search operator to obtain the Fortinet VPN login pages"

docs.title: Generated Shell Command
docs.text:
lynx --dump "http://www.google.com/search?q=inurl:%22remote+login%22+fortinet+OR+fortigate+OR+%22ssl+vpn%22" \
  | grep "http" \
  | cut -d "=" -f2 \
  | grep -o "http[^&]*"
